#1079. Amid protests, France's rising debt costs threaten stability

France plans to spend an extra €4 billion on education amid nationwide protests. But with public debt mounting and interest costs climbing, how much fiscal room does the government have?

Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.

The spread acts as a kind of "fever gauge" for bond markets, explained Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide toward a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he said.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fueled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE [the French national statistics agency — Editor's note], 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.

For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.

The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warned the economist.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In France, however, economic realities seem to have little impact on political debate. Both the far-right National Rally (RN) and the far-left France Unbowed (LFI) are campaigning on costly promises.

RN leader Marine Le Pen, for example, wants to reinstate the retirement age of 62 while promising €140 billion in savings. Jean-Luc Melenchon, LFI's leader, has even suggested that government bonds held by the French central bank should be "thrown into the fire."

"Nobody will ever notice they've disappeared," he has claimed.

For Heinemann, this is "a good example of radical parties on both the right and the left simply telling economic fairy tales."

Their common message, he said, is that "there is a way out of this mess that requires neither fiscal consolidation nor painful cuts."

Charrier is convinced that many French people have yet to grasp the seriousness of the situation.

"The euro has made it easier for France to access cheap financing and has long softened the pressure to adjust," he pointed out.

"In the past, currency devaluations [of the French franc — Editor's note] made economic imbalances immediately felt through declining purchasing power and rising prices. Today, that warning signal is missing. This has created the illusion that necessary adjustments can be postponed indefinitely," Charrier said.

This article was originally written in German.

#1077. Inside Stoke City's turnaround under Mark Robins: How they cleansed 'toxic' dressing room, the medical guru who stopped their injury crisis, a transfer expert armed with Brighton's secrets - and why they won't fall away like last season

Published: 21:00 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 27 November 2026

Stoke City have been here before. They know how it feels to be among the pace-setters, striding towards the place where they once belonged. They know, too, how easy it is to fall away.

At this stage last season, their first full campaign under Mark Robins, they sat second in the Championship. Would it be their year, a return to the top flight after seven years away, seven years in which they had finished in the bottom half of the Championship every season? It would not. They won three of their last 20 matches, none of their last six, and ended up 17th.

Victory for Stoke – who finished in the top half of the Premier League for three seasons in a row in the 2010s, remember – over Millwall on Wednesday night, their fifth on the bounce, sees them second again. Beat West Ham this weekend, who haven't won in six, and it's time to dream. Will this be their year?

Before a ball was kicked, Opta’s supercomputer had Stoke as the most likely team to be relegated. Robins, however, said things ‘felt different’. Speaking to those around the club this week, there’s a genuine belief they are.

Not that anyone would have thought it three months ago, when a 4-1 thumping at Wolves – a third straight defeat to start the season – left them bottom.

Club bosses wondered whether a change might be needed. The mood in the stands was starting to shift. There had been little appetite to sack Robins in the summer, but now the questions of whether they made the right call crossed a few minds.

Despite a dismal end to last season, and a poor start to this, Stoke stuck with boss Mark Robins - a decision that is paying off

Jack McGlynn leads the celebrations during Stoke's 2-1 victory over Millwall in midweek. They sit second in the Championship

After spending £30million on players over the summer, selling them the vision of what the club was building under Robins, it was felt sacking him before the window had even closed would be a dreadful look.

Stoke stuck by Robins, beat Norwich on deadline day in a gutsy backs-to-the-wall performance, and haven’t looked back since.

One thing that did change after the Wolves defeat, even if it wasn't the manager, was the formation. Sorba Thomas, the club’s leading scorer last season, was sold to Hull for £8million. Not only did it allow Robins to cash in on a player who made it clear he wanted to leave, but also to switch to a wing-back system that now gets the best out of the squad.

Robins and sporting director, Jon Walters, the former Stoke striker who felt the brunt of fan frustration following their collapse last term, have gone about building a club and culture that can finally succeed. The past few seasons have been spent shipping out plenty of rubbish and bringing in players with the right character and mentality.

Insiders talk about how ‘toxic’ the dressing room was just a couple of years ago, and how the standards set were ‘ridiculously low’.

A staggering injury crisis helped wreck their promotion hopes last season, so this summer the club revamped the entire medical department.

Damian Roden, the head of sports science during their Premier League days, returned as head of medical and performance. The club’s Premier League heroes of yesteryear, the likes of Ryan Shawcross and Robert Huth, have hailed Roden as one of the key factors in them finishing ninth three times on the spin under Mark Hughes. Roden’s periodisation model, which adjusts training volume and intensity to keep players at their freshest for match day, underpins Stoke’s weekly schedule.

He’s been joined in the medical bay by Matt Ratcliffe and Mark Sertori, who spent more than a decade at Manchester City and was recently head performance for Roma. So far, Stoke have only had a couple of muscle injuries.

John Coates, co-owner of Stoke (left), and sporting director Jon Walters have found a formula that is working as the club chase a return to the Premier League

George Hirst scores the second of two goals against Millwall. The son of Sheffield Wednesday legend David has been working with Robins, a former striker, on his finishing

The change in the Football League’s financial restrictions from the old-school Profit & Sustainability Rules, which capped losses over a rolling three-year period, to the new Squad Cost Ratio that allows clubs to spend a percentage of their revenue, has been a gamechanger for the Potters.

Suddenly, the shackles are off. Stoke have owners in the Coates family who put in as much money as they can. They recently opened a new £12m first-team building at their Clayton Wood training ground, which boasts a gym, swimming pool, hydrotherapy and cryotherapy suites and a tactics room for video analysis.

Now, they can spend on the squad too without worrying about being hamstrung by losses from previous years. They hope to bring in more players in January. The squad value has soared from around £30m a few years ago to more than £100m now.

Stoke are also finally starting to reap the rewards of their bespoke data-led recruitment model, following in the footsteps of Brighton and Brentford. Like those two clubs, Stoke’s owner John Coates – son of Peter, who founded bet365 – has vast experience in the gambling industry. Their head of recruitment Ian Torrance helped set up Southampton’s ‘Black Box’ scouting database and used data from Tony Bloom’s Jamestown Analytics during his time at Italian side Como.

Nearly all their signings this summer have hit the ground running. Ethan Galbraith, brought in from Swansea in a deal worth up to £10m, already looks like one of the best midfielders in the Championship.

Jack McGlynn, one of two players signed from the MLS alongside Luca Bombino, has been another revelation in midfield and already has five league goals. Justin Devenny brings Premier League experience from Crystal Palace.

Defender Luke Graham, snaffled from Dundee for £2m, has been a rock at the back and has earned his first Scotland call-up. Former captain and centre back Shawcross, one of Robins’ first-team coaches, has worked extensively with Graham, analysing video clips.

Ethan Galbraith, brought in from Swansea in a deal worth up to £10m, already looks like one of the best midfielders in the Championship

McGlynn, signed from the MLS, has been another revelation in midfield

Robins, a former Manchester United front man, has been doing one-to-one work with striker George Hirst, who joined for an initial £6m from Ipswich. That’s paying off, too. Hirst scored the winner against Birmingham last weekend and both goals against Millwall in midweek.

Stoke paid compensation to hire Arsenal Under 21s coach Max Porter, who helped bring through Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri and Max Dowman with the Gunners. He is in charge of how Stoke move the ball in possession – and appears to be doing a fine job.

The big question, especially after last season’s tail-off, is whether they can sustain this form. Stoke are, on the face of it, overperforming their underlying numbers. Opta’s expected table, which calculates where a side should  be based on their expected goals (xG), has Stoke 16th.

The feeling inside the club, however, is that in games where Stoke took an early lead and looked to defend it, it was always likely their opponents would rack up shots and xG.

If you look at Stoke’s rolling xG average, too, Robins’ side are starting to consistently create more than their opponents. Even if they were getting lucky earlier in the season, they aren’t anymore.

Their first-half performance against fellow promotion chasers Birmingham was hailed by those inside the club as the best Stoke have played in years.

No goalkeeper has kept as many clean sheets as Viktor Johansson, one of the most reliable stoppers in the division

Insiders feel the squad now has the depth to deal with any injuries that do come their way. Midfielder Djibril Soumare came off against Birmingham and is expected to be out for a while but they have plenty of cover. Galbraith missed two games and Stoke won them both.

Fans, for the first time in years, are going into matches expecting to win. They have one of the meanest defences in the Championship. No goalkeeper has kept as many clean sheets as Viktor Johansson, one of the most reliable stoppers in the division.

Stoke’s realistic aim is to finish in the play-offs. They have 35 points so far and know the average to finish in the top eight is around 69. It would need near-relegation form not to achieve that from their last 29 games.

Stoke have been here before. This time it feels different.

#1075. ‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Mathematics Álvaro Lozano-Robledo thought the Riemann hypothesis was out of AI’s reach for now.Credit: Bri Diaz/UConn Photo

The news came on a Friday — and it was ground-shaking. For months, reports have mounted of artificial-intelligence models toppling some of the toughest problems in mathematics, plunging the field into turmoil. But the latest claim was the most shocking yet: an AI model had helped to solve the field’s most famous open problem, the Riemann hypothesis.

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

AI is ‘the end of mathematics as we know it’ — where does the field go next?

The proof was released on 20 November by mathematician Levent Alpöge at AI giant Anthropic in San Francisco, California, who used an advanced version of the firm’s Claude model. It came in the form of 17 million lines of code in the open-source programming language Lean, which translates mathematical arguments into computer-certifiable code. In a matter of hours, a separate set of mathematicians rushed out a human-written proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which is in the branch of number theory and pertains to the randomness of prime numbers.

Alpöge’s proof has been independently verified by the non-profit organization behind Lean and the Mathlib Initiative, which runs the reference library of formalized mathematics results written in Lean. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him,” the community said in a statement on 21 November.

The mathematics community has broadly accepted the claim, although responses differ wildly. Some celebrate Alpöge’s achievement, but others see the development as proof that humans are fighting against machines for the future of mathematics.

Nature hears reactions from five mathematicians on what solving the Riemann hypothesis means to them.

Mathematician Tasmin Chu is part of the Association for Human Mathematics, whose members commit to doing AI-free research.Credit: Elizabeth Xiao

Tasmin Chu, PhD student in mathematics at the California Institute of Technology in Pasadena.

A technology that can autonomously prove the Riemann hypothesis is no trivial matter. I think that it is imperative our society acts to pause AI development as soon as possible. Over the past year, mathematical institutions have faced the impossible task of adapting to the rapidly changing capabilities of AI in real time.

It’s enormously disruptive for early-career researchers — the people who are the intellectual future of our field. Soon other sectors of society will face the same issues.

My reaction is grave concern. AI companies urgently require democratic oversight. I do not think AI’s encroachment into math is inevitable, nor is the death of human mathematical practice inevitable. It’s a choice to disempower ourselves, just as it’s a choice to continue building these technologies despite grave safety concerns. I continue to practice mathematics without LLMs, because I believe it’s critical that scientific inquiry continues in the hands of human beings. Some of us at the Association for Human Mathematics — whose organizing committee I am on — are collectively making the same decision.

Harini Desiraju, lecturer in mathematics at the University of Warwick, UK.

Given the events of the past few months, this news wasn't entirely a surprise, but we need to wait to understand the Lean proof and let the experts verify it. It is several million lines of code, after all.

I am not a number theorist, so I might not have the same emotional attachment to the Riemann hypothesis. Nevertheless, I have deep appreciation for the ubiquity and the importance of the problem in several areas of maths and physics.

As for the recent events, I want to distinguish between formal proofs versus knowledge. It is an impressive feat to solve such a problem. However, because it is a Lean proof over millions of lines, it is going to take a while before the community gets real understanding, and validity of the proof. With an AI-independent approach available as well, it could present a great opportunity for discovery of new ideas and mathematics. We need to see how it all plays out.

There is another discussion to be had, which involves the role of frontier labs in research. Most of us see the potential benefits of this technology, but it is of utmost importance that we work towards a future where the agency is with the scientific community and not a couple of companies.

Mathematician Marcus Du Sautoy is anxious about what’s next for his field.Credit: David Levenson/Getty

Marcus Du Sautoy, mathematician and professor for the public understanding of science at the University of Oxford, UK.

It was real mix of emotions. A part of me says, how exciting to be alive when this great problem was solved! I think even when Fermat’s last theorem was solved, we had the same excitement and the same melancholy: that great motivator is gone.

Mixed in with that, is the complete surprise that it ended up being proved this way. If you’d asked me three months ago, I would never have predicted it.

There’s quite a lot of anxiety about what ‘math 2.0’ is going to look like.

Xin Zhang, assistant professor in mathematics at the University of Hong Kong.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03835-0

#1074. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

The other factor which seems likely to condemn Sage is his team’s boneheaded defensive lapses. Another header conceded.

Formerly hated rival scoring against you, rubbing it in with his celebration: truly one to show the grandkids.

Liverpool had put together little of substance until then, with Wirtz drifting through another half, Alexander Isak looking keen but flawed and Barcola spooning a promising shot into low-Earth orbit. Isak had his moment in the end, checking back to finish calmly at the end of a counter-attack against a tiring defence. Eight for the season for him and an assist for Wirtz, too, although it was hardly a pass of Molbyesque majesty.

“Happy for him,” Iraola said of Wirtz, also praising Isak’s movement for the German’s goal. “I think [Wirtz] has been very unlucky in the Premier League, a couple of goals disallowed and situations where he deserves honestly to score.”

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.

#1071. How Andoni Iraola made Liverpool's fans - and players - fall in love with him: 'There's a connection building. He gets the club'

Published: 21:00 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 21:00 EST, 27 November 2026

The first sign that Andoni Iraola was different came this summer in Chicago during Liverpool's pre-season tour.

Sitting in a conference room up in the clouds overlooking the Windy City skyline and out to Lake Michigan, Iraola relaxed into a chair and held court for the best part of an hour. It was his first interview with the assembled Merseyside media corps but felt more laidback and personable than most of those chats tend to.

Most managers have little time for outsiders but Iraola, sipping a black coffee, was happy to stay put and talk about modern football, life in the Basque country and cycling. Only some of that conversation made the cut for the write-up but it all painted a clear picture of the new Liverpool boss.

Four months later, the Anfield faithful are slowly falling in love with Iraola.

It’ll take plenty more time and trophies to reach the adoration they had for Jurgen Klopp but, if Iraola can get halfway to that level, he will have done well.

So ahead of his first Merseyside derby, how has Iraola settled in at Liverpool – and why are the fans taking to him in return?

The Anfield faithful are slowly falling in love with their Spanish manager Andoni Iraola

Iraola takes training in Chicago on Liverpool's pre-season tour. The manager was relaxed during that time despite the pressures of a move to a huge club

It’s the little things that have helped Iraola forge a bond with the Kop.

He has been spotted on the parks of Merseyside taking in Sunday league football. He took his young daughter to a Women’s Super League game and attends her netball matches. And he has taken time to learn about the history of the club and the city, with incognito visits to tourist hotspots.

Iraola and his wife came to Liverpool on a city-break long before he became manager and loved the feel of it; it was a reminder of his hometown Usurbil, near San Sebastian in northern Spain.

He also enjoys cycling, a lifelong hobby, and his helmet helps him go unrecognised on rides around the city.

At the AXA Training Centre, there is a feeling of unity. Virgil van Dijk is a regular at academy matches, Dominik Szoboszlai dropped in on an age-group side last week and first-team players are tutoring youngsters and tracking the teams' scorelines.

None of the above might feel noteworthy in isolation but, to Liverpool fans, these little signs of a joined-up club mean the world. This is a unique fanbase which is often misunderstood: they want people who ‘get’ the club and the city. By immersing himself in them, Iraola is achieving those small wins.

‘There’s definitely a connection building between us and Iraola,’ says Dan Clubbe of fan channel Redmen TV. ‘First and foremost, matters on the pitch are starting to get exciting and the belief is growing as a result.

‘But beyond that, he’s very likeable and although it’s a cliche, he seems to “get it”. Small as they may seem, things like the WSL game, getting out to grassroots footy, integrating youngsters... that all resonates with us as fans.

‘It even goes beyond that. He seems to genuinely love it (here) and wants to understand better the opportunity he’s got, the place that he’s in. It’s still early days but it feels like he realises the significance and responsibility of his position.’

This time last year, the wheels were starting to fall off for Arne Slot. Liverpool felt like a fractured club

Tensions were rumbling around Mohamed Salah, who kicked off publicly and said the club had thrown him ‘under the bus’

This time last year, the wheels were starting to fall off for Arne Slot. Just six months after a Premier League trophy parade through the streets of the city, Liverpool lost 4-1 at home to PSV Eindhoven to record their ninth loss in 12 games, also including a 3-0 defeat by Nottingham Forest at Anfield.

Tensions were rumbling around Mohamed Salah, who in early December kicked off publicly and said the club had thrown him ‘under the bus’. He was dropped from a matchday squad and his relationship with Slot never really recovered. He is now at Turkish side Trabzonspor.

The best way to describe the feeling around the club last season was fractured. Sources point to how Slot kept the same outlook when things were going badly as he did when they were going well.

The place needed a fresh outlook. Iraola was the leading candidate to succeed Slot, though the hierarchy also assessed Pierre Sage, who has since been hired and fired by Crystal Palace, and Sebastian Hoeness of Stuttgart.

And then there is Iraola’s faith in youth. Rio Ngumoha, 18, and Trey Nyoni, 19, have been trusted to perform by the new boss. Lewis Koumas and James McConnell have been getting the nod in squads ahead of senior pros Federico Chiesa and Wataru Endo.

Iraola, who is superstitious and tapes his fingers before games for this reason, knows the significance of this week: having thrashed Manchester United and won away in Europe against a decent Club Bruges side, a Merseyside derby win would complete a trio of fantastic results.

Florian Wirtz this week thanked Iraola for helping him rediscover his best level

‘It’s a little bit like here – you know a lot of people on the other side,’ he said on Friday, comparing the clash with Everton to the derby between his boyhood club Athletic Club, of Bilbao, and Real Sociedad, of San Sebastian.

‘I have a lot of friends who are Real Sociedad and they have a lot of friends who are from Athletic.

‘There is always banter throughout the season and everyone wants to finish above them and win the games against them. It’s quite a natural rivalry. The relationship between them is normally quite good but everyone wants to win that game.'

Iraola went on to add that he is very happy in Liverpool, which he described as an ‘easy’ way of life. It will certainly feel that way if he completes the perfect double of beating Manchester United and Everton in the same week.

#1069. As COP31 Antalya kicks off, can world move beyond big promises?

Droughts, floods and extreme heat are upping the pressure on delegates at the UN climate talks in Antalya, Turkey. Can countries move beyond pledges to concrete action?

With its pulsing music, flashy images and barrage of special effects, the key message in Antalya's marketing video is clear: Turkey, the host of the 31st edition of the UN climate talks, is cool, stylish, modern — and eco-conscious.

Both President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and his wife, Emine, make an appearance, with Turkey's first lady calling climate change "one of the most visible manifestations of the burden human activity has placed on our planet."

From November 9-20, delegates from nearly every country in the world are coming together in the Mediterranean city of Antalya to chart a way out of the climate crisis. Turkey is the official host, and Australia will lead the negotiations. But the issues they'll confront during those 12 days are far more serious than the showy marketing campaign make them out to be.

Severe drought, extreme heat, wildfires and record-low water levels in Europe's main waterways — summer across the continent was dominated by climate emergencies.

And in late August, a series of flash floods triggered by a rock-ice avalanche in Nepal and Tibet washed away entire villages, killing more than 1,400 people and leaving thousands missing. Climate experts have linked the disaster to melting ice and a warming climate.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Globally, carbon emissions are still rising: the UN has concluded that it is no longer possible to keep global temperature rise to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial levels, the goal agreed at COP21 in 2015.

The global transition away from polluting fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas will be at the center of attention in Antalya — once again. To date, there's been no consensus on whether and how to transition rapidly away from this main source of global warming.

Despite the setbacks, the world has made some progress thanks to the 2015 Paris Agreement.

David Victor, a climate expert at the University of California San Diego, pointed out that before then, the planet was hurtling toward an average temperature rise of between 3-3.5 C.

If current climate commitments are fully implemented, the latest UN projections show a rise of up to 2.6 C. It's a significant step forward, even though warming of that magnitude will still have worldwide consequences.

"There's no question that we could be doing more," said Victor, though he cautioned against pinning too much on this year's summit.

All agreements at COP need to be unanimous, meaning individual states can quash any sweeping resolutions. Added to that challenge are the ongoing wars, trade conflicts and other economic problems swirling around this year's negotiations.

"It's like a giant Christmas tree in which everybody's hung their different ornaments, and the tree is groaning and more ornaments are being put on it," said Victor. "We have to look at it for what it is: It's a place where people talk about stuff."

Instead of waiting for all COP member states to agree, Victor sees a better chance for change in what he called "clubs" — smaller alliances of governments and companies working together to advance actual solutions, whether it be in aviation, shipping or electromobility.

"The Paris process is important. It has to go forward," he told DW. "But all the work is going to be done in clubs."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An example of this approach was last April's first ever International Conference on Transitioning Away from Fossil Fuels in Santa Marta, Colombia.

Colombia and the Netherlands invited representatives from 57 countries and key sectors to discuss ways to move the world away from coal, oil and gas, after an agreement on a similar plan failed at the 2025 climate summit due to opposition from several oil-producing states.

With an eye to the ongoing trade conflicts and energy crisis, hosts Turkey and Australia have included green industrialization and the clean energy transition among their aims. One goal is to increase the share of electricity in global energy consumption to 35% by 2035, up from around 20% today.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A recent analysis by the International Energy Agency found accelerating electrification could cut fuel-importing countries' energy bills by more than $400 billion (€357 billion) by 2035, compared to 2025 levels. The idea could appeal to regions dependent on fossil fuel imports — among them Germany and the European Union.

Ahead of COP31, German Environment Minister Carsten Schneider said Germany and the EU wanted to spark new momentum in the "global phaseout of fossil fuels."

It's wouldn't just be good for the climate, but a chance for many countries to boost their economies and reduce dependence on energy imports, added Schneider in a statement.

Oil-producing states like Saudi Arabia, however, aren't interested in deals that will undermine their business model. At recent UN climate conferences, they've repeatedly blocked any final agreements, including phaseout plans.

Even China, despite its massive expansion of wind and solar energy over the last 20 years, could be against the idea. The economic superpower traditionally rejects any outside demands, proposals or interference concerning its national decisions on energy policy.

Every country in the world is affected by climate change, with loss and damage calculated in the hundreds of billions from heat, drought and storms. Worst hit are vulnerable countries in the Global South and island nations, who are at risk of disappearing as sea levels rise.

That's where money comes into play, with developing countries calling for more support to protect their citizens from the harms of global warming. At the 2024 UN climate talks in Baku, Azerbaijan, industrialized nations agreed to free up at least $300 billion annually in climate financing by 2035.

But where exactly all those funds will come from remains hotly debated. At the same time, several major developed countries — most notably, the US — have cut their development aid.

The German government only paid out €4.7 billion from its 2025 budget for international climate financing, down from €6.1 billion in 2024.

"The level of financial support for developing countries today is far from what's needed," said Jan Kowalzig, a climate expert at Oxfam Germany.

Breaking financial promises like this comes at the expense of losing the trust of developing countries and, as a result, the diplomatic power which Germany and other industrialized nations rely on to shape policy to fight climate change.

Cosima Cassel, who focuses on climate diplomacy at the independent think tank E3G in Berlin, believes Turkey's push to turbocharge electrification during an oil crisis could be successful.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

For Cassel, a successful outcome at what are expected to be difficult negotiations in Antalya would reveal actual political will behind the grand agreements.

When it comes to electrification, that means taking the expansion of electricity grids and battery storage capacity seriously — not to mention removing the barriers to further electrification.

This article was originally written in German.

Yang Ji is in the Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China, and at the Key University Laboratory of Metabolism and Health of Guangdong, Southern University of Science and Technology.

Peng George Wang is in the Department of Pharmacology, School of Medicine, Southern University of Science and Technology, Shenzhen, Guangdong, China, and at the Key University Laboratory of Metabolism and Health of Guangdong, Southern University of Science and Technology.

Long chains of sugars known as polysaccharides support many biological functions, from strengthening tissues to modulating cell signalling. Synthesizing these compounds in the laboratory with precise lengths and architectures, which are needed to establish how the structures of polysaccharides affect biological behaviour, has been difficult. Writing in Nature, Yin et al.1 now report an enzyme-based strategy that produces highly uniform polysaccharides and enables chains to restart growth after consuming all of the sugar building blocks in the reaction, once more sugars are added. The authors achieved this control by adjusting how readily an enzyme binds the small sugar molecules that are used to initiate the growth of each chain.

#1065. 'Never Again!': Holocaust remembrance under pressure

Only a few Holocaust survivors remain who can share their stories firsthand. Meanwhile, voices calling for an end to what they describe as a "cult of guilt" are growing louder. How can Holocaust remembrance survive?

Young people pose inside a crematorium oven at the Buchenwald concentration camp memorial, laughing while they give the Nazi salute and take pictures of each other. "In a sense, they're trophies to post on social media for them to boast about — breaking the ultimate taboo," Jens-Christian Wagner, director of the Buchenwald and Mittelbau-Dora Memorials Foundation, told DW.

"Incidents like this have become more frequent in recent years. We have seen memorial trees planted in honor of concentration camp victims cut down. When something like this happens — and it happens regularly — I find it particularly despicable because, because it ultimately kills these people a second time," added Wagner.

Wagner is part of the curatorial team behind the exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in Bonn's Bundeskunsthalle, or the Art and Exhibition Hall of the Federal Republic of Germany. Wagner said Holocaust remembrance is under pressure, and the subject of intensifying attacks.

Critics have dismissed remembrance as a "cult of guilt" or "national masochism." With right-wing populism on the rise and historical revisionism becoming more common, Wagner worries about how Germany will remember the victims murdered by the Nazi regime. He is also concerned about the future of democracy. And soon, there will be no Holocaust survivors left to tell the true story of what happened.

This new exhibition tackles this concern head-on with numerous works of art and historical artifacts.

"I hope that perhaps even some people who don't already believe it's important to confront Nazi crimes will find their way to the exhibition," Wagner said. Memorial sites also attract visitors who aren't necessarily convinced of the need to confront these parts of history. Many of them are students.

"Let's not kid ourselves: When a teacher says 'We're going there,' it's always a mandatory visit," he said.

For today's young people, the Nazi era seems like the distant past, Wagner explained. "When you tell them to remember something that their grandparents didn't even experience, it naturally feels like an emotional burden. They can practically see the finger being wagged at them, and that doesn't exactly encourage learning."

A two-hour lecture won't have much of an impact if pupils aren't even paying attention. Instead, Buchenwald organizes full-day programs that allow students to explore historical sources together and make sense of history for themselves.

The next step, Wagner said, is to show young people that this chapter of history isn't closed. Visitors are encouraged to make connections between the past and current events like migration, for example.

"For the longest time, people have been discussing migration almost exclusively in terms of threats to public safety and crime. This broadly marginalizes certain groups — a mechanism that also worked for National Socialism," he said.

Eva Umlauf, 83, knows firsthand what it means to experience exclusion in its most extreme form. She is a patron of the Bonn exhibition.

In November 1944, Umlauf was just 2 years old when she, her pregnant mother and her father were deported by the Nazis from the Novaky labor camp in Slovakia to Auschwitz-Birkenau, the notorious Nazi concentration and extermination camp. She was saved from the gas chambers by mere days; the Nazis stopped using the chambers as the Red Army advanced, hoping to hide evidence of their crimes.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The camp was liberated on January 27, 1945. Three months later, Umlauf's sister Nora was born. But her father, her mother's siblings and her grandparents were all murdered. Eva barely survived herself. She suffered from tuberculosis, rickets and whooping cough, as well as edema caused by starvation. "Forget about the child. She won't survive," a doctor told her mother. But he was wrong.

Her mother returned to what was then Czechoslovakia with her two daughters, settling in Trencin. Eva Umlauf has no conscious memories of Auschwitz, but she carries her family's trauma deep within her.

Her mother never talked about what happened. Even so, Eva knew from an early age that she was a survivor. Her family rarely mentioned the camp by name, but one sentence came up again and again: "They stayed there." Eva knew that meant "they" were dead. And then, there was the number tattooed onto her arm: A26959.

Her mother taught her daughters not to draw attention to their Jewish identity — antisemitism was widespread throughout Czechoslovakia at the time. The small family managed to avoid harassment.

Eva Umlauf wanted to become a pediatrician, so she studied medicine. In the 1960s, she met her future husband, Jakob, who had also survived the Holocaust. He was an architect, active in Munich's Jewish community. They married in 1966, and she moved to Germany. She could hardly have imagined that she would one day live in the country of the perpetrators. "I don't hate Germans," she said. "But I cannot forgive. How can you forgive the deaths of 6 million people?"

It wasn't until much later that she first spoke publicly about the horrors of her early childhood. In 2011, she delivered a commemorative speech in Auschwitz on the anniversary of the camp's liberation. Since 2025, she has served as chair of the International Auschwitz Committee. A heart attack in 2014 motivated her to write her first book. "I was in intensive care. I thought to myself: If I get out of here healthy, I'll write a book."

Her memoir, "The Number on Your Forearm is Blue Like Your Eyes," was first released in 2016. The English translation followed in 2024. Since its publication, hardly a day has passed without someone asking Eva Umlauf to share her story.

She is appalled by the disrespectful behavior of young people at former concentration camps and by growing ignorance about the Holocaust. Sometimes, people even ask if she's too old to have a tattoo. But she also recalls a young man on the Munich subway who noticed the number on her arm and told her: "I want to apologize to you for what my ancestors did to you."

Umlauf never imagined that antisemitism would once again become so widespread in Europe and the United States. Nor did she expect the rise of Germany's far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.

"I go into schools. I'm so overwhelmed by the number of requests asking for my availability. And yet, the AfD is growing faster than I can reach students. It makes me think all this work is for nothing," she told DW.

Germany must never again fall under a right-wing dictatorship, she stressed. "'Never again' sounds nice, but all I can say is: It's happening again! Wouldn't 'Here We Go Again: Never Again' make a good title for the exhibition?"

She also shared her message to young people in the exhibition catalog, "Never Again": "You are not responsible for the crimes of your grandparents and great-grandparents. But you are responsible for the future. […] You are the generation that will shape our world. Make it a place where everyone can grow up safely, regardless of their background, faith or skin color."

She continues: "You don't have to be perfect. You just have to stay alert. Take care of your country."

The exhibition "Never Again! Against Forgetting the Crimes of the Nazi Regime" in the Bundeskunsthalle in Bonn runs through May 2, 2027.

This article was originally written in German.

#1064. How Southampton showed a lack of 'class' in bitter win over Middlesbrough after Spygate scandal: Star taunts fans with celebration and Kim Hellberg mocked to leave Tonda Eckert angry at his own club

Published: 16:57 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 01:13 EST, 28 November 2026

Southampton embarrassed themselves in their first meeting with Middlesbrough since the Spygate scandal as tempers flared at St Mary’s.

The club conducted themselves disgracefully in a bitter reunion six months on from their ejection from last season’s Championship play-off final.

Ryan Manning tucked James Bree’s cutback past Radek Vitek on 59 minutes to open the scoring for Saints before attacker Finn Azaz brought the contest to boiling point.

The former Boro forward scored Southampton’s second goal late on and then ran the length of the pitch to goad the away supporters by pretending to cry.

It sparked a fracas as Azaz and Will Lankshear - who wasn’t even at Boro last season when tensions were at their highest between the clubs - squared up, while travelling fans tried to get over the barricade.

Speaking after the match, Azaz said: 'They sang about me home and away last season, so I was just waiting for my moment to get one back. I have no regrets whatsoever.'

In a bitter reunion, Ryan Manning tucked James Bree’s neat cutback past Radek Vitek on 58 minutes before Azaz added a second as Southampton remained unbeaten at home in 10 months. Saints, though, were needlessly provocative throughout.

The scenes calmed post-match but Southampton’s off-field operation humiliated the club - taking their celebration too far.

Southampton's Finn Azaz mocked Middlesbrough's fans by pretending to cry after scoring

His celebration - in their first meeting since last season's 'Spygate' - sparked a brawl, with Azaz being booked

Hellberg cried in his press conference at Southampton last season when Boro lost in the play-offs semi-final before being reinstated. Saints reminded him of that incident by playing Oasis' Stop Crying Your Heart Out over the speakers. Throughout the match, the Saints fans sang: 'We saw you cry on the telly.'

Shamelessly, they added a box of tissues to the podium in the press conference room, which mortified Eckert, who removed them before Hellberg gave his post-match remarks.

‘I hope everyone who came here from the Middlesbrough staff knows that these things don't come from me,' Eckert said after removing the box of tissues, having stared at them for 20 seconds.

‘Everything you do in defeat and if you win you do in class and I try to do that. I hope that there's an appreciation that this doesn't come from me.’

Hellberg added: 'In general, those who show more emotions and stand up for what is right are brave people. Hiding behind people and being afraid of emotions, that's the problem we have in the world a little bit.

'We have to hide from everything, how people are feeling, mental health and everything. It’s important we stand up for that – I'm not afraid of showing feelings.'

Saints beat Middlesbrough in last season’s play-off semi-final but were booted out by the EFL four days before the final after Daily Mail Sport revealed Southampton had sent their very own Johnny English to spy on Boro’s training sessions.

Both managers called for an armistice before the match but that memo clearly hadn't reached the Southampton marketing team, who posted an inflammatory video on social media.

Hellberg cried in his press conference at Southampton last season and a box of tissues were shamelessly added  to the podium in the press conference room after today's match

The uncouth 79-second film mocked Boro, with the narrator declaring, ‘they got another go, their story continued’ over footage of Oli McBurnie’s winning goal for Hull City in the play-off final was also projected onto the big screen just eight minutes before kick-off.

'I didn't like the video this morning,’ Eckert said. If we look back a couple of months, the reality is both clubs have lost.

‘One club has lost off the pitch, and the other club has lost on the pitch. It’s an episode that is good to close for both clubs to move forward.

#1062. Chelsea bullied by Brian Brobbey and Sunderland

Talk about cramming everything in. Brian Brobbey only played for 67 minutes but, in that time, he collected a yellow card, ripped Levi Colwill’s shirt and earned himself a standing ovation after morphing into a battering ram.

Régis Le Bris, Sunderland’s head coach, said there was nobody like the Netherlands striker in the Premier League and it said everything that everyone wanted to make Brobbey centre of attention after a long overdue home win, even though he had not scored. Everyone, that is, bar Xabi Alonso.

“No, he’s not unstoppable,” Chelsea’s head coach replied when asked why his team had found Brobbey too much to handle. “He’s stoppable – but only when you defend better than we did. We were not bullied. We didn’t produce enough.”

That is one way of putting it. Another would be to say Brobbey was everything that Chelsea, much to Alonso’s disgust, were not: a bristling menace, a steamroller wearing a pair of boots, a player on a mission to help transform the mood – Enzo Le Fée’s decisive spot kick owed everything to Brobbey.

Chelsea arrived on Wearside looking to establish themselves in the top four ahead of the break but, instead, Alonso watched through his fingers as Sunderland reminded everyone why they were the joyous story of last season, a beautiful mix of inspiration and perspiration.

In fairness to the Chelsea manager, he refused to get caught in the minutiae of contentious penalty decisions – one that Chelsea were denied, another that they conceded – and could only lament as Sunderland ground out their first Premier League win since August 30, 70 long days ago.

“It wasn’t the best game,” Alonso said. “I think that we didn’t deserve more than probably one point, maybe. We need to be more consistent on the move, to get the ball from one side to the other, and we didn’t do that good enough. We didn’t produce enough to deserve to win.”

Unlike Sunderland. If you had turned up at the Stadium of Light without looking at the Premier League table, you would not have believed the hosts were bottom and you would not have given credence to the idea Le Bris, who has worked miracles these past two years, was under pressure.

Things, however, could not have started worse for Le Bris. Though Granit Xhaka has not shown last season’s form in these challenging opening months, the game plan was built around him, so to see the Sunderland captain hobbling off after three minutes was symptomatic of how things have gone for the Wearsiders.

“He felt something in the final sprint of the warm-up,” Le Bris explained. “We don’t know how bad it is.”

He is not the kind of coach, though, who will bemoan bad fortune. Le Bris sent on Jules Ahoka to replace Xhaka and watched as he, along with colleagues in red and white, set about trampling all over Chelsea’s intentions with incessant hard work.

Yet there was more to it. Sunderland can play, either intricately or directly, and a lovely move in the 12th minute needed a desperate, sliding intervention from Pep Chavarría’s to stop Trai Hume’s volley sliding in at the far post.

In the next attack, another Chemsdine Talbi cross – the Moroccan having been found by a peach of a pass from goalkeeper Robin Roefs – invited Brobbey to inflict maximum damage, but the Dutchman made a hash of his opportunity.

So close for Brobbey! 🤏 Sunderland almost take the lead against Chelsea. https://t.co/CUE6jHbPH2

The momentum could have changed completely in the 23rd minute. Alonso, his players and staff were convinced they would be given a penalty after Cole Palmer tumbled when his legs tangled with Luke O’Nien but, after a lengthy delay, VAR Nick Hopton felt there was no case to answer.

Hopton was involved again in the 33rd minute but, as Alonso said, Chelsea only had themselves to blame. Colwill simply could not contain Brobbey when he began marauding, grappling, grabbing and clipping the Dutchman’s heels. Le Fée did the rest, sending Mike Penders the wrong way.

From that point, Chelsea were in trouble, no matter how many changes Alonso made. They huffed, puffed, but nothing worked. They had come up against a red-and-white wall, fortified by constant backing from the stands, and the west Londoners were never going to knock it down.

One incident, as the clock ticked towards 90 minutes, encapsulated everything good about this Sunderland display when O’Nien chased down substitute Geovany Quenda to make a challenge. Another moment of defending from Thomas Meunier on Morgan Rogers was exceptional.

“You could see our identity and our togetherness and the way we managed the game,” said Le Bris, who was booked when hectoring referee Jarred Gillett. “These three points were critical. It was a struggle at times to manage situations. We showed as a group real heart.”

And nobody did that more than Brobbey. No wonder Le Bris will be hoping Xavi Hernández, the Netherlands head coach, handles him with care over the next 10 days. On this form, he will be the fuel that drives Sunderland’s quest for survival.

“How you do – good or not – it is a matter of staying together. The international break is coming so the lads can be calm in the head and when we all come back we need to be motivated to go again.”

For Sunderland that argument is easy to make – they are bottom of the Premier League, are without a win since August and for morale, if nothing else need at least a point, though three is really what the doctor orders.

For Chelsea – fourth in the table and with three wins in their past four league outings – the argument that this is a must-win game is harder to make, but bear with me here...

Facing a Sunderland team who are suffering from the worst of both worlds – blunt in attack and pitiful in defence (what a difference from last season...) and have proven all too easy to beat (as their 2-0 home defeat Zagreb illustrated on Thursday) – the west Londoners are expected to win. Fail to return to the capital with the three points and there will once again be question marks over Xabi Alonso’s side. They are flaky and flashy in equal measure, able to play and win well in spurts, but once again unable to mount sustained pressure needed for a title challenge and forced to battle it out for the hope of a top-four spot at best. Those will be the arguments raised should they not win this afternoon.

The hosts doubtless wish that their ‘issues’ were as golden as today’s opposition. For Trai Hume, who scored in this fixture last season, the Sunderland players are at fault for the sorry start to the season and he wants to put right the wrongs so far, starting today.

“I couldn’t tell you what’s changed. We thought we’d addressed it after the Leeds game, where we were aggressive, strong, but we go out there tonight and see the old habits of the start of the season. Everything’s a bit laboured, and it’s something the staff can’t fix, it’s on us as players,” Hume said.

“We’re still together as a club, as a team. I think the run of form we’re on, it would be easy to think we’re not, but we are. We are really upset with how we’ve been playing, and the results don’t lie. We haven’t been good enough and we know that. We have to address that.”

#1060. Why Nvidia CEO's affair with alleged Chinese spy matters for AI race

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has apologized for an affair with a woman the US believes was spying for China. The story could have profound implications for the world's most valuable company and the global AI race.

Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang's admission to an affair with a woman whom US intelligence officials believe was working as a spy for China could have profound implications for the $5 trillion (€4.47 trillion) company.

The Financial Times first reported on Huang's affair with Alice H., an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based customer of Nvidia, which has been suspected of trying to circumvent export controls to get advanced Nvidia chips into China.

The newspaper reported that the US government and its intelligence community believe she was recruited as a spy by China's Ministry of State Security intelligence agency.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

US government officials drafted a memo about the allegations shortly before US President Donald Trump traveled to Beijing for a summit with Xi Jinping in May.

Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese spy has exposed him and the company to criticism that it may have allowed China to obtain valuable trade secrets as Beijing tries to gain an edge in the race to develop advanced AI models.

Nvidia is initiating an investigation led by independent board members and an external law firm. It said in a statement that Huang "has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort."

"The board prioritizes US national and economic security, which is paramount to the interests of Nvidia and its shareholders," the company said Sunday. "While the board has no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised, the board's inquiry will examine all available information."

The company's shares fell in early trading on Monday.

While US intelligence officials have not commented publicly on the claims, Trump — with whom Jensen Huang has a close relationship — has backed the Nvidia boss.

"He's an honorable guy," said Trump. "I have not spoken to him ​about it. I just know he's a ​fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything's fine."

Tim Culpan, an Asia tech reporter who has covered Nvidia and Huang closely for years, told DW that while Nvidia's fundamental strengths as a company remain in place, Huang is hugely personally damaged by the story.

"They're still going to make great chips and they're going to sell them to millions of customers around the world who want the best AI chips in the world," he said.

"His opinion is going to carry a lot less weight now. And that, in the long term, will flow through to Nvidia and Nvidia's own corporate interests. So it won't be immediate. It's really a fact that he doesn't have the sway or the power that he might have had one week ago simply through this."

Richard Windsor, a tech analyst and the founder of research company Radio Free Mobile, said the news could be very serious for Nvidia given how much the company has revolved around Huang for decades.

"This problem is particularly acute because Jensen Huang is very hands-on, meaning that the key decisions that led to its success were ultimately taken by him and because there is no obvious successor," he said.

"I suspect we are about to find out just how much the market thinks that the company is dependent on its iconic founder and CEO."

Nvidia and Huang's attitude toward China and potential Chinese customers has been a bone of contention with US intelligence officials — despite Huang's close relationship with Trump.

Huang has repeatedly lobbied Trump to ease restrictions on the sale of Nvidia chips to China. A 2025 export control deal heavily curbed sales, but Trump subsequently permitted the export of older H200 Nvidia chips to China in return for the US government receiving a cut of the sales.

However, that deal has been complicated and bogged down by Washington's strict export-license review. China has also initiated import controls, despite strong demand from Chinese companies. China lacks access to the most advanced AI-capable chips. Beijing wants to develop its own alternatives but has struggled to catch up.

Huang has argued that Chinese dependence on Nvidia's chips would prevent rivals such as Huawei from catching up and boosting China's ambitions to dominate AI supply chains.

However, that argument has been dismissed by many US intelligence officials. They fear that unlimited Chinese access to the most advanced Nvidia chips would boost China's domestic AI sector, lead to its AI models catching up with the leading US models and see the chips being used in Chinese military applications.

The US-China rivalry has become a central theme in the global AI story, with both countries seeking to gain an upper hand in the technology. Leading US AI executives such as Anthropic's Dario Amodei have argued that US AI companies can't afford to take a prolonged pause to allow safety standards in AI to catch up, if they're going to prevent Chinese firms from gaining an advantage.

Washington's central fear over Huang's affair is that it could have led to Beijing obtaining vital trade secrets or other key information about how Nvidia makes its most advanced chips.

Windsor thinks Huang will survive the "severe test" due to his importance to the company. He also cast doubt on the extent to which Beijing and its leading tech firms have learned from Nvidia's chips, pointing to China's own chip ambitions and commitment to have its firms buy its own semiconductors.

"I am far from convinced that Chinese AI has materially benefited from technology or illicit chip imports that it gained from Nvidia," he said.

The news comes at a particularly challenging moment for Nvidia, which has benefited massively from the AI boom thanks to its position as the leading maker of cutting-edge semiconductors needed for AI applications.

Nvidia's valuation has soared dramatically in recent years as companies rushed to buy its chips, becoming the world's first $5 trillion company in October 2025.

However, doubts over the sustainability of the $9 trillion capital expenditure AI boom have sparked a major sell-off in stocks related to the boom in recent weeks. The Democrats' sweeping victories in the US midterms have added to the doubts, given the strength of voter opposition to data center construction in the US.

Sometimes playing ‘knee football’ down there. Or competing in what they called the ‘BYFL’ – the ‘back-yard football league’ they set up among themselves and neighbours. ‘They all loved sports,’ says their mother, Linda.

Of course, the British form of football doesn’t feature.

This homespun scene contrasts with the family’s current dismay about the chaos created at Manchester United, which has led to renewed discussion among several of the siblings about selling off some, or all, of their shareholding.

Most of the siblings consider selling a minority share to Sir Jim Ratcliffe to have been a mistake, according to a source with a social connection to the Glazers. Though there is not a sense of how the family feel about individual Ratcliffe appointees, they are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold – former United commercial director and chief executive, whose part working on dozens of commercial deals saw him oversee around £4billion of revenue.

American football - and their team the Tampa Bay Buccaneers - is the Glazers' true love. Joel Glazer led the celebrations when they won the Super Bowl in 2021

The Glazers have been ‘surprised’ at the loss of other influential senior staff, according to the source.

Arnold saw the writing on the wall before Ratcliffe and Ineos arrived. He personally negotiated his own exit with the Glazers. But they were then unable to prevent other departures which have been detrimental to the club, according to sources with no Glazer connection who have worked with United.

Those lost include the highly respected Victoria Timpson, United's former 'CEO of Alliances and Partnerships', who struck the Snapdragon and Teamviewer shirt sponsorship deal, but left in December 2024.

Florence Lafaye, former United commercial director, briefly took over Timpson’s responsibilities but also left to join Timpson in establishing the commercial agency Altius8, which was soon hired by Tottenham Hotspur.

Joel, Avram and Bryan Glazer are the three siblings thought to relish owning United – a calling card they have used at, among other settings, the Davos World Economic Forum, where United were the only football club to take a pavilion in the past.

Joel, whose 10.7 per cent shareholding is the biggest of the six siblings, was often seen as a man of interference before Ratcliffe’s arrival, pushing for higher fees when executive vice chairman Ed Woodward or others were trying to negotiate a transfer sale.

But the interest in United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie is far less certain, even though all six sit on the United board and Darcie holds the second largest share at 9.71 per cent.

The six collectively wanted to test the water for a sale after seeing US financier Todd Boehly pay £4.25billion for Chelsea in 2022. They formed the impression that United could sell for twice that much.

The interest in Manchester United of Kevin, Ed and Darcie Glazer (pictured) is far from certain, even though all six sit on the United board

The original plan was that Ratcliffe would ultimately buy the rest of United for £4bn, but since buying into the club, his chemicals business has been hit by a prolonged industrial downturn, collapsing profitability and high energy costs.

The Ineos Industries division recorded a £1.84bn pre-tax loss in 2025, his chemicals empire is carrying more than £10bn of net debt and he has been exiting from most of his sports interests.

The Glazers have the power, under the terms of their deal with Ratcliffe, to sell the club outright and force him to sell his stake. Another option would be to divest themselves of a small slice of their 48.9 per cent stake. But the current uncertainty about the future landscape of the Premier League created by the Manchester City case, with a slew of possible legal cases in its wake, is impacting on outside investment in top-flight clubs.

The family may have to sit tight and hope the recovery of the club’s fortunes, allied to plans for a new £2bn stadium, will take the club’s value closer to the £6bn that the six would be likely to agree on as an exit figure. They could tap into the bond market as Barcelona did to finance their $1.5bn upgrade of Camp Nou, or look to private equity funds, who would want a major pay-back when the stadium is built.

But for the first time through their 21 years as owners, United face the frightening predicament of relegation – bringing, for example, a £5.7million-a-year TV deal in the Championship compared with the £191.5m in Premier League income banked last season.

With new Premier League Squad Cost Ratio rules allowing the club to spend 85 per cent of last year’s £677.6m revenue on players and £160m in the club’s rotating credit facility, there is money.

Multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny

The Glazer family are thought to rue the departure of Richard Arnold (pictured), the club's former commercial director and chief executive

Multiple sources say the Glazers stepped in to ensure Mauricio Pochettino’s appointment – something United deny. But the source close to the family also believes they will now continue to present a greater challenge to what many see as Ratcliffe’s running down of the United operation.

The Bloomberg report showed how Ratcliffe’s 300 job cuts had focused heavily on commercial, media and administrative divisions, which former employees said had eroded relations with corporate partners and caused a deterioration in the level of service.

A former executive described how long-standing sponsors, accustomed to receiving complimentary autographed merchandise, were told they should expect to pay shipping fees for signed memorabilia. ‘Penny wise, pound foolish,’ the executive said. This was certainly not the Glazer way under Woodward and Arnold, who built that side of the operation.

The Glazers are 47th in the Forbes list of most wealthy US families and the Amazon Tampa Bay Bucs series reveals an innate obsession with the financial bottom line and making profit. ‘My father didn’t give a damn about what anybody else thought,’ Ed Glazer tells the film-makers. ‘He would always say, “Why can’t we do this?”. We could look at anything as long as the numbers made sense.’

It’s hard to believe that Ratcliffe, a man desperately trying to preserve his own business, is going to get in the way of the Glazers seeking ways to preserve the long-neglected asset which is now staring into the abyss.

#1054. Rare gene variants can affect a person’s height by up to 17 centimetres

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Chris Simms is a science writer based in Somerset, UK.

Human height is determined almost entirely by an individual’s DNA.Credit: XinXinXing/Getty

Rare mutations that prevent proteins from functioning can have a surprisingly large effect on people’s height, researchers have found.

An analysis of more than 1.4 million people’s protein-coding DNA has identified hundreds of genes that affect people’s height. The work also uncovers previously unrecognized biological mechanisms that underly human growth.

The findings, published on 25 November in Nature1, might help with the development of treatments that mitigate height changes caused by some medical conditions, such as forms of dwarfism.

“The impact these genes have on any given individual can be massive in terms of accurately predicting their height or making sure they’re getting the right treatment for a disease,” says Adam Locke, a statistical geneticist at the Regeneron Genetics Center in Tarrytown, New York.

About 80–90% of variation in adult height is caused by genetics. Projects analysing common gene variants have mapped thousands of DNA changes that can influence height. For example, a 2022 study identified more than 12,000 common genetic variants that collectively accounted for 40% of height variation in populations with European ancestry2.

However, how rare genetic variants (those found in less than 1% of a population) affect people’s height is less well studied.

To systematically probe how rare variants contribute to people’s stature, Locke and his colleagues gathered DNA and height data. In total, they looked at sequencing data from more than 1.4 million adults. They analysed the protein-coding sections of DNA and ran a series of tests to spot non-random links between height and both common and rare gene variants.

The analysis uncovered rare variants in 207 genes, which, on average, were linked to a height difference of about two centimetres. The team also identified 17 genes that had a particularly strong effect on height. The variants associated with this gene set all resulted in the production of non-functional proteins. In the study, over 700 people had at least one of these loss-of-function variants.

Genetic study homes in on height’s heritability mystery

Genetic study homes in on height’s heritability mystery

Individuals carrying such a variant were, on average, about nine centimetres taller or shorter than were people who didn’t have that variant. The strongest effects included a 17-centimetre reduction in height associated with a change to the ACAN gene and an 11-centimetre increase linked to the FBN1 gene. These effect sizes are more than 50 times larger than those of most genes commonly associated with height.

“We would expect rare genetic variants that disrupt gene function to have larger effects than common genetic variants, but the magnitude of some of these effects is particularly striking,” says Andrew Wood, a statistical geneticist at the University of Exeter, UK.
