Source: P. J. Klasse et al. Nature Rev. Microbiol. 23, 734–752 (2025).

By harnessing potent antibodies that can vanquish diverse viral strains, scientists are closing in on one of the most elusive goals in biomedical research: a vaccine for HIV. This year, several research teams described vaccination strategies that triggered the production of these broadly neutralizing antibodies (bnAbs) in monkeys, and precursors to bnAbs in people, suggesting that an effective vaccine is possible. But devastating cuts to US funding for HIV research have left some efforts in limbo.

The world is closer than it has ever been to an effective HIV vaccine. It also has a drug capable of preventing infections: the long-acting injectable drug lenacapavir, which could avert an estimated one-third of new HIV infections in Africa if given to just 5% of adults. Now is the time for funders to ramp up investment, not cut it back, argues a Nature editorial.

Reference: UNAIDS & Gates Foundation report

Pregnancy causes drastic changes to the brain, but we know little about them because of past worries about the safety of scanning pregnant people. Now, researchers are working to fill that void by collecting scans from first- and second-time mothers and analysing thousands of archived brain scans acquired during routine clinical care. The work, presented last week at the US Society for Neuroscience annual meeting, could help to explain maternal mental-health conditions such as postpartum depression.

‘General purpose’ artificial-intelligence tools such as OpenAI’s GPT and Anthropic’s Claude are impressing researchers with their emerging biology skills, including protein design and structure prediction. In some tests, these models have even outperformed those designed specifically for biology tasks and trained on vast troves of protein-sequence data. Some scientists predict that generalist AI tools could eventually catch up with, or surpass, blockbuster models such as AlphaFold. Others suggest these new abilities could be the result of regurgitating training data, rather than advanced learning.

As I write, the United States army is preparing to detonate around 4.4 tonnes of unstable lead azide, a chemical used to make munitions, at an ammunition plant in Iowa. “It's essentially a lead bomb,” says occupational and environmental health researcher Patrick O’Shaughnessy. “Now it's a matter of how much gets ejected out of the bunker.” Academic researchers have banded together to gather independent public data about the plume of toxic lead dust that is expected to spread over the area.

Figure 1 | Position verification. a, To check the location of a party called the prover, two verifiers each send a random bit (a challenge), which are timed to reach the location simultaneously. The prover combines the bits and returns the answer. Because no signal travels faster than light, a prompt reply shows that the prover is at the location. b, However, if two adversaries, one near each verifier, copy a challenge and pass it to each other, they can answer in time even though nobody is at the claimed location. c, In Kavuri and colleagues’ scheme, one verifier generates two entangled photons, keeping one and sending the other to the prover. Both verifiers then transmit classical challenges. The prover uses the challenges to determine how to measure its photon and returns the result, while the first verifier measures the other photon. If the prover’s result arrives in time and the two measurements pass a statistical check (a Bell test), the transmitted photon must have been measured at the claimed location.

“Banks, power grids and satellite-navigation systems all depend on knowing where a request or a signal comes from, yet claims about location are notoriously easy to fake,” notes physicist Davide Bacco. Now researchers have outlined an experiment in which the position of a distant party is certified using quantum entanglement.

In a, two verifiers send random bits (challenges) timed to reach the claimed location simultaneously. The prover combines them and replies. Because signals cannot travel faster than light, a prompt response verifies the prover’s location. But two adversaries (b) can defeat this test by exchanging the challenges and responding in time. In (c), a verifier also sends one of two entangled photons, which are inexorably linked in a way that can be proven using a statistical check (a Bell test). If the prover’s result arrives inside the time window imposed by the speed of light and the photons pass the Bell test, the prover must be inside the target region. (Nature | 9 min read)

Chemist George Whitesides made landmark contributions to many fields, including patterning surfaces with molecules — a technique that enabled ‘lab on a chip’ diagnostic devices — advances in nanotechnology and more. He prided himself on switching research interests often, telling students, “If somebody else is working on something, don’t work on it.” In traditional chemistry departments, “there’s often a lot of pressure to stay in your lane, and he made it okay not to”, says polymer scientist Joseph DeSimone. “In fact, he made it exciting not to.” Whitesides has died, aged 87.

Read Whitesides’s guide to writing a scientific paper in a special issue of Advanced Materials that celebrated his 65th birthday.

Some mental disorders seem to take different forms in different places, writes mental-illness researcher Alexander Pereira. “Even depression – arguably the most common psychiatric condition in the world – seems to look strikingly different depending on when and where it appears,” he writes — with bodily symptoms, such as fatigue, prevalent in China, and psychological symptoms, such as low self-esteem, more common in the West. Pereira argues that our ability to adapt to our social environment might significantly shape the internal mechanisms of mental health.

Changing location — even just walking through a doorway — can signal to our brains that work is over and it’s time to relax, says cognitive scientist Joan Ongchoco. (BBC Future | 11 min read)

Reference: Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology paper

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03879-2

The stunning geological formation was buried in the 1886 eruption of Mt Tarawera, but it will never be forgotten.

#946. Klopp wants Infantino out as FIFA candidate deadline looms

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has joined the chorus of football figures critical of FIFA President Gianni Infantino. But with time running out, there are few who seem willing to run against him.

Germany coach Jürgen Klopp has become the latest prominent football figure to call for change at the top of FIFA.

"Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job," he said on Sunday.

But with time running out before the November 18 deadline for new candidates for the presidency of world football's governing body, Infantino is looking overwhelmingly likely to win another term.

"There are people who truly care about the future of football, people who aren't driven by financial interests," Klopp said ahead of Germany's Nations League match against the Netherlands on Monday.

"If someone like that were to step up — if someone like that were to become president — I think that would be a significant improvement."

If that person is waiting in the wings, they're leaving it late to step on the stage. Despite a raft of federations and continental confederations, including Germany, UEFA (Europe), CONCACAF (North and Central America and the Caribbean) and AFC (Asia), calling for Infantino's head in the wake of his plan to sell off part of the World Cup earlier this year, the incumbent appears to have stopped the bleeding.

That plan, which involved forming a subsidiary arm of FIFA called FIFA Forward Enterprise (FFE) in order to sell off part of its commercial operations to investors including Joshua Kushner — brother of US President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner — was widely panned before being abandoned.

It followed on from widespread criticism of Infantino's awarding of a new FIFA Peace Prize to Trump, the overturning of a red card for US national team player Folarin Balogun, and with Trump's involvement, at the World Cup and a host of other controversies.

Since then, though, many public critics have backtracked amid FIFA promising to release an extra $2.7bn (€2.45bn) from its reserves over the next four years to the federations, increasing their total investment to $6.35bn.

Perhaps the most significant of these u-turns came from the AFC, who went from saying Infantino had committed a "fundamental breach of trust" in August, to offering the Swiss its "full commitment to supporting you and your leadership as you seek a new mandate as the FIFA president" in October.

Those words were spoken by AFC President, Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who ran against Infantino when he first won the top job at FIFA in 2016. He will not run again and said that "my feeling is, I'm sure, the feeling of most of my members," in regard to Infantino.

Proof that the sentiment is not universal comes in the shape of Kozo Tashima, the honorary president of the Japan Football Association (JFA). Tashima is one of only two people to confirm they will oppose Infantino in the March 2027 presidential elections.

The 68-year-old is a well respected figure in Asian football politics and will have no problem meeting the threshold of support from five of FIFA's 211 federations. This is not like the other candidate, former Swiss international player Ramon Vega, who is an enormous outsider. Tashima appears to be running on the basis that he will be able to chart a calmer path at FIFA.

"I am grateful that I can make this announcement with the full support of the Japan Football Association," Tashima told the Japanese newspaper Sports Nippon. "It's not about winning or losing but about conveying to the world the honest, sound and upright attitude that Japanese football has built. What FIFA needs now are these values that we have protected. I have decided to run in order to make this appeal to the world."

But the numbers are against him. Though support from within the confederations may not be total, the backing of AFC and the African confederation (CAF) is a huge boost for Infantino, with those two alone making up 101 votes, almost enough for a majority.

In fact, the only real concern remaining for Infantino remains UEFA. The European federation, headed by Aleksander Ceferin, is a major revenue source for FIFA but the two organizations are at loggerheads. As well as a war of words, UEFA are seeking to obtain evidence for a potential Swiss criminal case against Infantino in regards to FFE. FIFA have called this a "smear campaign" and a "fishing expedition".

But, so far, UEFA has not put up a candidate. Former Arsenal coach turned FIFA Chief of Global Football Development, Arsene Wenger was thought to be a contender but has now ruled himself out. Wenger's compatriot, Philippe Diallo, has since emerged as another option, with The Guardian reporting on Monday that the French Football Federation president could be announced on Tuesday.

While Europe is football's powerbase, particularly from a club perspective, UEFA will need Diallo, or any candidate they can convince to run, to win votes from outside its 55 nations to have any chance of success, particularly with Tashima likely to split any challenge. Even if a candidate appears before the November 18 deadline, Klopp's hope for change appears to be a long shot.

#944. COP31 draft deal calls for 'immediate' shift away from fossil fuels

The preliminary agreement at UN climate talks in Turkey calls for a rapid reduction of planet-warming emissions and at least $120 billion to help countries adapt to climate change.

COP31 co-host Australia has kicked off the second week of climate talks in Antalya with a draft political deal calling for an "immediate transition away from fossil fuels" and a "tripling" of finance for climate adaptation measures in developing countries to at least $120 billion (€109 billion).

The goal of other co-host Turkey to increase electrification of the world's economies to 35% by 2035 also features in the text. The draft emphasizes clean energy but notes that "electrification can provide co-benefits regardless of the electricity mix" — an approach that has proved divisive at the talks, with many insisting that electrification be strictly tied to renewable energy.

Language around a faster phaseout of oil, coal and gas is important because fossil-fuel producing nations have repeatedly pushed back against stronger wording in previous COP decisions.

"The new negotiating text contains all the necessary building blocks for a successful outcome to the conference: from the goal of climate neutrality for all industrialized countries by 2030 to a work program that can keep the 1.5-degree limit in place," said Greenpeace Germany head Martin Kaiser on Monday.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The draft expressed "deep concern" that the 1.5 Celsius (2.7 Fahrenheit) temperature threshold agreed at the 2015 COP in Paris to avoid runaway climate change was now out of reach. It stressed the need for "accelerating action to minimize both the magnitude and duration of any temperature overshoot and to return global warming to below 1.5C as soon as possible."

Recognizing a need to address rising carbon emissions, the draft highlighted efforts to "urgently and rapidly" scale up controversial technologies to capture and store CO2 to bring down atmospheric carbon levels.

"For the first time, all the parties here are grappling with the fact that the world will inevitably exceed 1.5 degrees. Negotiators must deliver a response," said Ani Dasgupta, president of the World Resources Institute, adding that this meant going beyond slashing emissions.

"This requires scaling carbon removal through both nature-based solutions like restoring forests and wetlands, or emerging technologies that directly capture carbon from air," he told reporters.

Kaiser, however, criticized the lack of binding commitments in the draft's resolutions. He added that Europe should work with China and the most climate-vulnerable countries to keep oil-producing nations, including Russia and countries in the Middle East, from "undermining the conference's decisions and turning them into a free pass for the oil and gas industry."

Other activists have dismissed carbon capture as a "false solution" being promoted by corporations.

Cosima Cassel, an expert at climate think tank E3G, was cautiously pleased with the draft's "ambitious language" but said it appeared the broad deal would now leave negotiators to "fight for trade-offs."

"The test will be whether the final decision keeps the core elements once that process plays out: ambition on overshoot, defense of the science, clean electrification and forward progress on adaptation finance," she said in a statement.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Disagreements over financing largely relate to who should bear the costs of international climate action, whether financial support should be provided through grants or loans, and how funding for developing countries can be increased.

Representatives of developing nations and small island states, regions bearing the brunt of the climate crisis, have protested climate inaction and a lack of financial support in recent days.

"Climate finance isn't an extra at these talks: it's the condition for everything else," said Rukiya Khamis, program manager for East Africa with environmental group 350.org. "It's alarming how financial pledges by wealthy, polluting countries are dropping like a stone — COP31 must stop this with a strong outcome on adaptation finance."

"Now we must fight to keep this [adaption finance] in the final decision and ensure these promises become real, grant-based money," said Harjeet Singh of the Fill The Fund campaign, which calls on rich countries and corporations to deliver the funding needed for climate-related loss and damage, such as homes destroyed by floods and harvests ruined by drought.

"Communities are suffering devastating losses and damages today precisely because we failed to deliver adaptation at the right time," added Singh.

At 18 pages and 144 items, the draft will be the focus of lengthy discussions in the coming days as delegates try to come to an agreement by Friday. Some observers went so far as to say the document's scope was too wide to be taken seriously.

"The draft final declaration reads like a Christmas wish list," said Niklas Höhne, a climate policy expert at the NewClimate Institute in Germany. "There are even several points on which we will obviously not be able to reach a consensus, including for example the proposal that developed countries achieve net-zero emissions by 2030."

But Chris Bowen, chief of negotiations and Australia's minister for climate change and energy, appeared optimistic.

"The general tenor and tone [of the talks] has been very constructive," he told reporters Monday. "Parties have come to me with strong views about various things, as you'd expect […] [but] they've also come in the spirit of cooperation, the spirit of respect and a spirit where parties have said to me that they want to help get an outcome."

David Waskow, director of WRI's International Climate Initiative, said the draft text showed a level of "seriousness" on important issues like finance, electrification, oceans, overshoot scenarios and emissions of greenhouse gases including methane, which has a warming impact more than 80 times stronger than CO2.

"The question is whether the level of ambition on those issues is carried through into the final outcome here," said Waskow. "And that's what we need to be watching closely over the coming days."

Additional reporting by Tim Schauenberg in Antalya.

Update, November 17, 2026: This article has been updated with additional reactions to the draft text.

Abhinand Lal is in the Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), Paris-Saclay University, 91190 Gif-sur-Yvette, France.

Daan Noordermeer is in the Institute for Integrative Biology of the Cell (I2BC), French Alternative Energies and Atomic Energy Commission (CEA), French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS), Paris-Saclay University, 91190 Gif-sur-Yvette, France.

Large regions of chromosomes are organized into a state known as heterochromatin. This densely packed form of DNA represses gene activity. Curiously, some families of clustered genes can be activated even though they are packed as heterochromatin. Writing in Nature, Buckley et al.1 report findings that explain this paradox: they show how opposing mechanisms that control the organization of heterochromatin promote the stochastic activation of genes in the protocadherin (Pcdh) gene cluster, thereby supporting proper nervous-system development.

#940. Underperforming Manchester City are an accident waiting to happen

Enzo Maresca had two home games in four days to get Manchester City into decent shape for Sunday’s clash against Arsenal, which now feels like a must-win. On Tuesday, however, they ended up being taunted by Rasmus Hojlund on another evening that raised more questions than answers.

It is now one win in seven for Maresca, who cannot keep a clean sheet and has a £327m midfield that have played well individually, but is yet to form a unit. Worryingly, their reliable source of goals, Erling Haaland, had his quietest game of the season. It required Rayan Cherki to rescue a point against Napoli.

Maresca needs to find a solution in the next five days before heading to the Emirates to face the champions in what could be a defining weekend for the season. Defeat would put them nine points off the pace, with Maresca still trying to find his best combination of players to pick.

Club captain Rúben Dias was on the bench here and Josko Gvardiol was left out of the draw against Fulham at the weekend, which also ended as a draw rather than a morale-boosting win to get City out of their slump.

There is enough quality in City’s midfield to trouble Arsenal, but the conundrum for Maresca is how to fit them all into his system. Elliot Anderson was pushed towards the right against Napoli rather than in a central position to control the game, while Ayyoub Bouaddi was often alongside “inverted” full-back Nico O’Reilly.

Bouaddi showed his attacking instincts with City’s first equaliser; incredibly his first goal as a professional. There cannot be many £86m players who have yet to score in senior football. Enzo Fernandez also started against Napoli but was quiet before being taken off for the last half an hour.

What a way to score your first senior goal 🤩 Ayyoub Bouaddi brings Man City back on level terms with a beautifully taken finish! 📺 Stream now on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/8UjQ5PSK8r

“Football is easy and difficult. When you win it’s easy and you know what to do,” said Haaland, who City have relied on this season. “When you don’t, you start questioning everything. The perfect thing would be to not think, but it’s not so easy.

“We have so much quality, so it’s about getting the quality out in every player. We have to regroup, stay positive and bring energy on the pitch and try to do our best.

“We go to the champions, so it’s the most difficult game of the season going to the champions away. We need a top performance from every single player.”

A penny for the thoughts of Khaldoon Al Mubarak and Aleksander Ceferin, who sat next to each other in the Etihad directors’ box.

Khaldoon has been the chairman of a club under siege after the Premier League found them guilty of breaking financial rules. They could be punished with a points deduction that would mean they miss out on the Champions League, the blue-riband tournament of Uefa, of which Ceferin is president.

Ceferin will want figures like Haaland and entertainers like Cherki to be playing among Europe’s elite, although this City team look far from contenders for this year’s edition. At the moment they will take any kind of win.

City were giving a debut to their new orange kit, but a change of strip did not bring a change of fortune. Their jerseys have been likened to Irn Bru, but the most of the running was made by Napoli, whose midfield was made in Scotland from girders. It was Billy Gilmour who set up the opening goal with an astute reverse pass for Hojlund.

Hojlund shouted at the crowd that there was “one team in Manchester” – his old club United – as he celebrated his goal. It was a sweet moment for the Denmark striker, who toiled for two seasons at Old Trafford before they looked to offload him. He has been at Napoli for two campaigns but the rivalry with City is still there.

The goal came from City trying to play out of defence again and making an error when it went forwards to Cherki. It resulted in another goal conceded and it is now 10 games in a row without a clean sheet. In seven of those they have conceded first, leaving them looking at ways to salvage a result

Jérémy Doku had been brought on as a sub seconds before Napoli scored, then played his part in Bouaddi’s equaliser. From a short corner, Doku pulled the ball back for his team-mate to finish with a first-time side-foot shot.

Noa Lang’s last trip to England came last season when his thumb was caught between advertising hoardings and needed it stitched back on. He had Napoli’s bench celebrating on the pitch when he thumped home a volley from Leonardo Spinazzola’s cross, finishing off a slick counter-attack.

Kevin De Bruyne has been lined up for a January move to PSV Eindhoven, with the Dutch club working on a deal to land one of the Premier League’s greatest players when the window opens.

De Bruyne, 35, has been at Napoli since the start of last season but it is understood that a move away from the Serie A club is now on the horizon. He is still under contract at Stadio Diego Armando Maradona so PSV will pay a fee to land him as they look to retain their Eredivisie title.

At Manchester City, De Bruyne won six Premier League titles and was part of their Treble-winning team that won the Champions League. During the last 18 months at Napoli he has suffered injury issues, had a row with team-mate on the pitch and was quoted as saying he was glad Antonio Conte left as head coach.

“Not a lot I can say for the moment,” said De Bruyne when asked about his future. “I have played at 100% until now and obviously I am not 20 years old, I am turning 36.

“There is a lot of things going in my mind but there is not a lot to say. I am playing good football, trying to help the team to do well and it has been a bit of a challenging season with a lot of things happening.”

It is matchday five of the Champions League as Manchester City host Napoli at the Etihad. These sides last met back in September 2025, with Manchester City winning 2-0 at home courtesy of goals from Erling Haaland and Jeremy Doku. Manchester City’s cause was helped by an early red card for Napoli’s Giovanni Di Lorenzo. Napoli’s only win over Manchester City came all the way back in November 2011 when they won 2-1 after a double from Edinson Cavani.

Manchester City have won three of their opening four Champions League matches this season, with their only defeat coming at home against back-to-back champions PSG. They drew 1-1 at home against Fulham in the league on Saturday, which means they are now without a league win in four games.

“We are always looking to win games, no matter the competition,” Manchester City boss Enzo Maresca said. “For sure, the four games in a row in the Premier League that we did not win has been a shame. Tomorrow [tonight] we have a chance to win the game and continue our path in the Champions League that at the moment has been very good. First of all, it is important to qualify and then probably, if you are not able to finish in the top eight, you have two more games that with the amount of games that we have, it is always important to reduce games. So the target is to try and finish in the top eight.”

Napoli, managed by Massimiliano Allegri, have struggled thus far in this season’s Champions League, winning just one of their opening four games and are all the way down in 27th. They come into tonight’s match off the back of a 1-0 home win over Torino in Serie A on the weekend courtesy of former Manchester United midfielder Scott McTominay’s winning goal. However, they still sit down in eighth in the Italian top flight, a massive 14 points off the top through just 12 games.

“This match will not be decisive,” Allegri said. “It is a simple mathematical equation, but obviously we will try to do well, even against a great team like Manchester City. It will be a beautiful and fascinating challenge and we want to play to the best of our ability. Ultimately, our goal is to qualify. We must not repeat the mistakes we made in Porto, where we played a great game for 70 minutes and then let ourselves go, conceding chances too easily. We will have to be able to play both with and without possession.”

Team news from the Etihad to follow shortly.

#938. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

In 1962, a martini-drinking womanizer saved the world for the first time in "Dr. No." As Robert Pattinson takes on the role of 007, here's how the films evolved.

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios announced on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival."

Based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond."

Shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

In principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

Although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

Whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

His pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral."

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

In the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary."

In the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian."

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

If there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

Now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17."

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

#935. China’s AI-powered smart-city model is going global

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Jacob Dreyer is an editor for business, economics, politics and law at Palgrave (a subsidiary of Springer Nature) based in Shanghai, China. The views expressed here are his own.

To understand the Chinese smart city, it helps to know that twenty-first-century infrastructure, technology and policy increasingly makes the whole of China a single, interconnected economic unit. Trains, planes and autonomous vehicles shuttle about, with the centre of megacities such as Shanghai and Shenzhen merely being in the middle of ‘one-hour circles’ for commuters that allow them to reach anywhere in the wider urban area with ease. Previous barriers to the internal movement of workers, such the hukou system, which restricted access to public services based on a person’s birthplace, are being removed, making it easier for people to compete for jobs across the country. And all the while, the Internet supercharges these shifts to a nationwide marketplace, backed by an ever-expanding supply of data centres. Sichuanese farmers of organic lemons now livestream from rural villages on apps such as Xiaohongshu or Douyin as they compete for city restaurateurs to buy their products.

So, if the goal of a ‘smart city’ is to use big data and AI to outsource governance functions, keeping everything running smoothly, then maybe we should think of China as a single city, with its different provinces and megalopolises as neighbourhoods with their own special roles. For instance, three of China’s megacities each have their own important function: Beijing regulates and invests in fundamental research; Shanghai is home to multinational corporations, frontier research in AI and biotech, and finance; and the Greater Bay Area, including Shenzhen and Guangzhou, is home to innovative manufacturers, such as electric vehicle producer BYD, tech giant Huawei and consumer electronics firm DJI.

China’s 15th five-year plan unveiled earlier this year sees the country in this way, too, by entrusting certain functions to different cities and regions, and with rural areas also playing an essential role. In the northeast, farming is increasingly carried out with the use of drones and big data by state-owned companies such as Beidahuang. In Inner Mongolia and Xinjiang, data centres are powered by abundant solar and wind energy, where they calculate how the self-driving cars of China’s eastern seaboard should navigate roads or process the AI that helps to keep the country’s state-of-the-art high-speed train network running on time.

This approach on data is embodied by 东数西算 (roughly translated as ‘east data, west compute’), a national-level strategic project to channel data from developed eastern regions to resource-rich western regions for processing and storage using eight data-centre ‘hubs’ located across the country. Eastern megacities generate the vast majority of China’s data and AI requests, but they bring skyrocketing land costs, power shortages and cooling difficulties that make hosting data centres unattractive. Instead, the solar farms of Xinjiang’s deserts and the wind farms of the Mongolian steppe are used to provide renewable, cheap energy to data centres.

One key example is Ulanqab in Inner Mongolia, which has been transformed from a traditional farming region into a prominent data powerhouse, earning the name ‘Grassland Cloud Valley’. The energy costs in Ulanqab are low, because the government has been installing massive renewable capacity, relying on the area’s abundant wind and solar resources. Mongolia is cold for most of the year, so data centres use standard air cooling rather than massive air-conditioning set-ups — effectively, they just cover the servers with plastic and leave the door open for wintry winds to circulate. Major firms such as Huawei, Alibaba, Kuaishou and Apple have constructed large-scale cloud bases in Ulanqab. The region houses China’s largest intelligent computing centre for autonomous driving (Fuyao), built by Xpeng Motors and Alibaba Cloud, which has helped make it 170 times faster to train self-driving models. It means an autonomous taxi driving around Beijing is effectively being controlled by servers in the far-away desert of Inner Mongolia.

The late Kevin Keegan thrashed home a free-kick at this stadium 50 years ago to win Liverpool the Uefa Cup and Sir Kenny Dalglish was the hero at Wembley in 1978 when his deft finish ensured the European Cup was retained.

That jersey means those who have subsequently worn it have had high standards to keep. Although this fixture did not carry the heft of past occasions, it was symbolic that Wirtz, the incumbent, decorated this contest and propelled Liverpool a step closer to the knockout phase.

On another night Alexander Isak would have expected his two goals to take the headlines, but he would have appreciated more than anyone the magic spells that Wirtz kept casting. The Swede had a glorious view of the strike that essentially secured three points in Belgium’s frozen north.

The idea of Brugge playing in the biggest club fixture of all, sadly, seems fanciful now given how much the footballing landscape has changed. But they are a progressive side, full of attacking wit, and they had ambitions and, on another evening, would have done some damage.

How often, though, do you see sides these days undo their good work by being overambitious when playing out from the back? Yann Sommer has had a distinguished career, the Swiss goalkeeper has played for Bayern Munich and Inter Milan, but he is 37 and his aberration was decisive.

He put Kyriani Sabbe in all manner of trouble with a loose pass, Bradley Barcola picked the right-back’s pocket and nudged it on swiftly to Dominik Szoboszlai, who in turn fed Isak. With the goal at his mercy from six yards, the striker was never going to miss.

Liverpool have travelled over to Belgium to take on Club Brugge on matchday five in the Champions League. These sides have met competitively three times before and they have all come in finals, resulting in famous nights for Liverpool. In 1976, Liverpool beat Club Brugge 4-3 on aggregate across two legs to win the Uefa Cup. Then, Kenny Dalglish scored the only goal of the game at Wembley back in May 1978 as Liverpool won the European Cup for the second straight season, becoming the first English side to do so.

Liverpool, who have won 13 of their previous 17 matches against Belgian sides, won their first three Champions League games, beating Atletico Madrid, LASK and Villarreal but lost 3-2 away at Fenerbahce on matchday four despite leading twice in that game. After tonight’s game in Belgium, Liverpool’s remaining games in the Champions League are against Porto, Inter Milan and Lens. Andoni Iraola’s side come into this game with a spring in their step after thrashing rivals Manchester United 4-0 at Anfield on Sunday.

“A win [against Manchester United on Sunday] is always great but you do not have time to celebrate with this schedule,” Iraola said. “By Monday, we were already watching analysis of Club Brugge. I have enjoyed analysing them [Brugge], they are very energetic and have had an incredible run of games. I think we will have to be at a very good level, otherwise it is going to be very difficult. They have players who can make the difference and obviously we do as well, so I expect quite an open game. We are both aggressive, both want to press, there will be spaces and hopefully we can win the one-vs-one battles.”

Club Brugge have made a strong start to this season’s Champions League; after losing their first game to Aston Villa, they have since won their next three, including wins over Inter Milan, Lens and PSV. That puts them on the same number of points as Liverpool and are just one place behind. In the Belgian Pro League at the weekend, they thrashed Mechelen 5-1 and they sit second in the Belgian top flight, one point behind Union SG.

“I am proud of the players and what they have achieved against Aston Villa, Inter, Lens and PSV,” Club Brugge boss Ivan Leko said. “We know we should be grateful to be here, but we really want to try to show that Belgian football is fun to watch and we can win matches. I am proud, but I know we are a big club. You are only as good as your last match. We know what happened in the past, so there is also a nice connection between both clubs and the supporters. It is a special fixture to play, but we are not here just to enjoy the Champions League; we want to win and that is what we are going to try to do tomorrow [tonight].”

#932. NASA's Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away from Earth

When just saying 'hello' takes a two-day round trip, you're a light-day, or 26 billion kilometers, from Earth. Only one human-made object has ever traveled that far — and its journey into interstellar space continues.

Hate long-haul flights? Well, imagine having to travel 3,300 years to get to your destination.

Imagine departing in 1977 and arriving in 2026, on November 18 at 11:16 a.m. Central European Time to be precise, and then, not stopping but continuing the journey.

NASA's Voyager 1, a spacecraft launched almost half-a-century ago, has traveled a light-day from Earth.

A light-day is the distance light covers in 24 hours — about 26 billion kilometers (or around 16 billion miles). Put another way: Light does in one day what it took the spacecraft 49 years, two months and 11 days to do.

But Voyager 1 is not only far away, it is also traveling at an incredible speed of 61,000 km/h (38,000 mph).

When Voyager 1 launched, it was in sync with a planetary alignment that was as rare as the spacecraft itself — one that happens only once every 176 years. It was the alignment Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, which scientists wanted to investigate.

Once the original mission was accomplished, Voyager 1 used the planets Jupiter and Saturn to perform a gravitational slingshot.

It flew close to each planet, got pulled and accelerated by their massive gravity, and swung around faster than before. And that is how Voyager 1 has achieved its speed.

In the vacuum of space, nothing slows you down.

On Valentine's Day 1990, from beyond Neptune, Voyager 1 took the only portrait of the solar system from the outside ever made by a spacecraft.

In 2012, it became the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.

Its journey is ongoing. In about 40,000 years — long after its plutonium power supply dies out — it will still be flying and pass by the star Gliese 445, which is more than 17 light-years away from Earth.

That's light-years, not light-days. A light-year is the distance light travels in a year. It will take Voyager 1 about 18,000 years to reach the one light-year milestone.

Voyager 1 is destined to wander the Milky Way "perhaps eternally," as NASA puts it.

The spacecraft is the first human-made object ever to be one light-day away from home.

"If you want to say 'hello' to Voyager, you send your message and then you go home and you wait two days before you finally get a response," says Suzanne Dodd, the mission's project manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory.

But you do get a response. Even today it sends back data that helps scientists on Earth.

"[It's] still working great, sending back data from a region of space no other human-made craft has ever explored," says Kareem Badaruddin, the mission manager at JPL.

No story about Voyager 1 seems complete without mentioning The Golden Record, a phonographic record, that is part of the spacecraft's cargo.

The spacecraft is carrying other Earthly objects as messages and artefacts from Earth for extraterrestrials. But the Golden Record is what we tend to focus on because it contains soundbites representing languages and cultures from around our planet.

We're told it's very unlikely that any intelligent lifeform will ever receive the cargo or even know how to play The Golden Record.

But if they do get the record and work out how to play it, the first thing they will hear is a controversial voice — not one of Earthly unity, as was the original idea. Those are the words of Kurt Waldheim, a former UN Secretary-General (1972-81) and Austrian President (1986-92), whose concealed wartime past as a German army officer in the Balkans surfaced a decade after Voyager 1's launch. It was alleged Waldheim had participated in Nazi crimes.

#930. France's Philippe Diallo to challenge Infantino for FIFA presidency

Philippe Diallo is the second candidate to stand against incumbent Gianni Infantino. He is backed by European football's governing body UEFA, known to be critical of Infantino.

French Football Federation (FFF) President Philippe Diallo has received UEFA backing to be a candidate in FIFA's presidential election, which will take place in March in Morocco, with criticism against current chief Gianni Infantino growing.

UEFA, European football's governing body, said it has backed Diallo "unanimously" in a bid to replace Infantino, putting it's "full support" behind the Frenchman.

Veteran Japanese official Kohzo Tashima has also announced his candidacy, with the deadline for candidates to stand for election being November 18.

Potential candidates for the post must show letters of support from five of FIFA's 211 member associations before going through eligibility and integrity checks.

Diallo, the 63-year-old head of the FFF, is the son of a Senegalese boxing champion.

He was elected as the federation's president in 2023 with a large majority. He was reelected for another four-year term in 2024.

Back in September, Diallo said the FFF had withdrawn its support for Infantino ahead of the March 2027 election, saying trust in the FIFA president had "been betrayed."

"The way in which the governance of world football is envisaged no longer reflects us," the French football head said of the decision.

If elected, the Frenchman would become FIFA's first black president, as well as it's third French leader after Robert Guerin and Jules Rimet, who served as the organization's first and third presidents.

Gianni Infantino has been in charge of world football's governing body since 2016.

He has been facing growing criticism since pitching a plan of sell a stake in the World Cup to private investors. The criticism of the plan was led by UEFA and its President Aleksander Ceferin.

Infantino ended up scrapping the plan but UEFA went ahead and took FIFA to court in the US, trying to gather evidence ahead of potentially lodging a criminal complaint with Swiss authorities about alleged "mismanagement" by Infantino.

FIFA's headquarters are located in Zürich, Switzerland.

Infantino was also criticized after creating a peace prize and awarding it to US President Donald Trump last year.

The connection between Infantino and Trump came under criticism once again during the World Cup, after United States forward Folarin Balogun was allowed to take part in the round-of-16 game against Belgium despite having been shown a red card in the previous game.

The US president admitted to having personally intervened through a conversation with Infantino.

#929. Gut microbes can adapt to our ageing bodies

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

John A. Lees is at EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute EMBL-EBI, Hinxton CB10 1SD, UK.

Our guts contain around 40 trillion bacterial cells, a similar quantity to the number of cells in the entire human body1. Although the community of bacterial species in the human gut usually stays relatively stable over time2, genetic mutations in such bacteria can be associated with a measure of body size called the body mass index3. Writing in Nature, Wang et al.4 scanned the gut bacteria of some 10,000 people for genetic variation and searched for statistically significant associations with almost 250 characteristics, including age, height and cardiovascular fitness. The authors singled out one adaptation that seems to help one of the most abundant bacterial species in the human gut to resist a form of stress called oxidative stress, which damages cells and increases as people age.

#928. One person had a worse night than United keeper – the wretched referee

By the end of another utterly chaotic 90 minutes in the Manchester United soap opera, there was only one person who had endured a worse night than Senne Lammens.

Watching this game back will make for grim viewing for the United goalkeeper who, having been one of the club’s shining lights last season, is steadily becoming enveloped in a crisis of his own in this most torrid of campaigns.

But Roberto Rosetti, Uefa’s chief refereeing officer, might also want to sit Szymon Marciniak down after this and pick over the Polish official’s own nightmare performance. Marciniak denied United two goals, both of which should have stood, and in doing so ended up shining an even more brutal lens on Lammens’s calamitous display.

United’s Belgian goalkeeper was responsible for both of Sporting’s goals. He needlessly conceded a penalty in the first half, after a rush of blood to the head, that was converted by Luis Suárez, just 75 seconds after he had saved a spot-kick from the Sporting striker.

United had recovered from those bewildering few minutes to lead early in the second half, courtesy of two goals from captain Bruno Fernandes against his old club.

But, 10 minutes from time, Lammens committed the kind of howler that becomes worse and worse with every viewing. In doing so, he handed Sporting an equaliser and ensured United remain without an away win this season.

Lammens could have come to meet Iván Fresneda’s cross 100 times and probably dropped the ball only once. It was his and United’s misfortune that it should happen here. Suárez could barely believe his luck, although his finish was still accomplished, an acrobatic overhead kick from close range.

Senne Lammens with a gift for Luis Suárez to equalise for Sporting 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/kOQ6HImlVc

One of the stars of last season for United, Lammens is being dragged down with the rest of them this time around. He had looked hesitant from the moment he was almost caught dealing with a back-pass by Suárez in the opening minutes. It set the tone for what was to come.

As if Mauricio Pochettino did not already have enough on his plate, United’s new head coach now has a goalkeeper problem.

Of course, this would not have been as costly a night for Lammens had Marciniak not made such a mess of things himself. United may have been their own worst enemies again, but there was little doubting Sporting were given a helping hand here by some truly wretched refereeing.

The worst of it was the denial of a perfectly legitimate equaliser late in the first half after Youri Tielemans was penalised for a perceived foul – it was nothing of the sort – that the referee had initially not blown for.

And then moments after Suarez made it 2-2, the Sporting goalkeeper Kaique Pereira flapped at Fernandes’s corner and punched the ball into his own net. Kaique’s blunder was already in motion by the time Patrick Dorgu barged into Kaique. But Marciniak was ordered to the pitch-side monitor by Piotr Lasyk, the VAR, and from there, he weakly decided Kaique had been infringed upon by Dorgu. It was a big let-off for the goalkeeper and the hosts.

To compounded United’s frustrations, they were then reduced to 10 men late on when Tielemans, who had been booked for protesting over the first disallowed goal, received a second yellow card. It means United have now had four red cards and conceded five penalties in their last five games and, four weeks shy of Christmas, are still searching for a win on the road.

The irony was that, amidst the chaos, there was a lot Pochettino will have liked about the performance. It was far from perfect but United at least had a structure, coherence and confidence about them for long periods. But for Lammens’s shocker and some dubious refereeing, United would surely have claimed just a fourth win this season.

The problem with this United side is they never seem too far away from an act of self-sabotage. Pochettino insisted on the eve of this game that his team were not fragile, but that assessment was challenged in the crazy 160 seconds when United conceded not one but two penalties.

In truth, they could feel hard done to by the award of the first in the 29th minute. Geny Catamo went down far too easily – and very late – after Lisandro Martínez swung out a leg. There was contact but it was of the very minimal variety. Martínez rushed off to Marciniak to remonstrate but his pleas fell on deaf ears. There was a sense of justice, then, when Lammens saved Suárez’s feeble penalty.

You would have thought that would be a confidence booster for Lammens, but in no time he had gone from hero to zero, with worse to follow.

A ball was swept in behind Noussair Mazraoui and Maximiliano Araújo gave chase. There was no need for Lammens to come careering out of goal but that is what he did. When he clumsily blocked off Araújo in the process, Marciniak wasted little time brandishing a yellow card and pointing to the spot. This time Suárez made no mistake from 12 yards.

What will please Pochettino is United did not crumble again from there. In fact, they rallied and would soon be nursing a sense of injustice for the second time in four days.

Already outraged by the circumstances around Leny Yoro’s rescinded red card against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday, Pochettino now had to contend with some perverse refereeing from Marciniak.

Tielemans had slipped a pass through to Amad Diallo, with his momentum carrying him into Gonçalo Inácio. Marciniak did not blow his whistle, presumably because in the moment he did not feel a foul had been committed. But after Diallo’s shot was saved and a split second before the Ivorian headed the rebound into the net, the Polish referee blew his whistle.

It's hard to know why this was ruled out 🤯 📺 Watch live on TNT Sports & HBO Max https://t.co/fRCRh6tXYB https://t.co/Pat8nzJiVW

Tielemans could not believe what he was seeing and, to add insult to injury, was booked for his protestations.

The problem for United was that, because Marciniak had blown moments before Diallo put the ball into the net, VAR were powerless to review the decision.

After the match, Pochettino claimed United were punished by the referee’s decisions.

The Argentine was again in a state disbelief at some refereeing decisions, even though he appeared at pains not to land himself in hot water with Uefa.

“It’s difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game. We were punished a lot in key actions,” Pochettino said.

On the foul awarded against Tielemans, he added: “I think everyone knows all that was… impossible [to understand]. You know, it’s difficult to understand why that happened on the field.”

What Pochettino demanded was a strong start after the interval, and he got just that. A third penalty award of the night this time went United’s way. Martínez, who had been operating as an inverted left-back for much of the game, wriggled his way past Eduardo Quaresma before being bundled over from behind by the Sporting defender. Fernandes stepped up and coolly converted the penalty. This time it was Sporting’s turn to implode, even if Fernandes and United’s goal had some good fortune about it.

Fernandes was running to the right when he cut back inside, just outside the penalty area, and struck a speculative left-foot shot at Kaique. There appeared no obvious danger and then the ball seemed to hit a divot in the ground, seemingly created moments earlier by Fernandes as he slid in, and cannoned upwards. The Sporting goalkeeper was thrown by it and the next thing the ball was flying through his hands.

United have had very little in the way of luck this season, so their supporters would argue it was long overdue. Misfortune, in the form of Lammens’s clanger and Marciniak’s refereeing, would soon come back to haunt them, though. What a job Pochettino has walked into.

A much better United performance, undermined by a terrible night for their goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who conceded a penalty and dropped a simple cross when they had a second-half lead.

Before that, there were hints of a Pochettino team in United’s football: they were industrious, energetic and fully committed, and they were the better of two limited teams for long chunks.

Manchester United, always the pressure is there, you compete for big things, one or another competition it is to win. That is the history of the club.

I was under the misapprehension that Peter Schmeichel and Michael Laudrup were Euro 92-winning team-mates with Denmark, but in fact Laudrup had a three-year hiatus from the national team and opted to stay away from the tournament when Denmark replaced Yugoslavia. One more in the win column for the Ewing Theory (that says teams can improve without their star player).

Laudrup told FourFourTwo: “As we weren’t able to qualify, I decided to focus 100 per cent on Barça. Yugoslavia went on to win the group, but because of the war, Denmark were suddenly given their place. People asked me if I wanted to go, but I didn’t want to join at the last moment, even though I could have. I felt it wouldn’t have been fair.”

Shaun Derry, the former Crystal Palace and QPR player, is in attendance to cheer on son Jesse who is on loan at Sporting from Chelsea. Heck of a loan move for a 19-year-old, and good to see him in fine fettle after that horrible head injury he suffered on his full Premier League debut season.

“Of course, minutes have been minimal for Jesse, but nights like this you can’t beat,” Derry said. “There are some great young players that he is learning alongside.”

“He wasn’t making his bed a year ago, now he has to cook his own dinner and get himself to training.”

Wandering around the Jose Alvalade Stadium before kick-off and Cristiano Ronaldo’s face and old No 7 is pasted on the outside of the building.

How Pochettino would love a prime Ronaldo in his team but we’re in as very different era now to the one when United went into this competition with a firm expectation of winning it. It’s two wins and two defeats so far in the Champions League for United this season although you suspect they’d be happy to come away from here with a point.

They have yet to win away from home this season and Sporting, who have won three of their four European games, are third in the Portuguese league. Watch out for Colombia striker Luis Suarez and Italy midfielder Issa Doumbia, who have six goals between them in the Champions League this term.

Harry Maguire comes in for Matthijs de Ligt, who was abysmal against Liverpool, and Noussair Mazraoui replaces Diogo Dalot. Amad Diallo is in over Patrick Dorgu. Mainoo and Tielemans have struggled as a partnership all season but Pochettino again persists with that midfield pairing with Bruno Fernandes ahead of them.

They need to finish 24th or higher to avoid elimination. They only have two fewer points (after four games) in the Champions League than they do in the Premier League (after 11).

Few Manchester United fans expected a positive result from Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge at Anfield, but the bar will not be set so low for Sporting in the Champions League this evening.

The manner of the 4-0 defeat against Liverpool, even accounting for Leny Yoro’s early red card, was dispiriting but not unexpected. The next few weeks will reveal how Pochettino intends to get a grip on the job.

When it comes to United’s Champions League prospects, the comeback win over Roma at the tail-end of Michael Carrick’s tenure made their position less perilous, but avoiding outright elimination is the first target.

United are 19th in the table, with the top 24 teams going through. Those between ninth and 24th go into a play-off round before the last 16. After Sporting away, United host RB Leipzig and Bayern Munich before a trip to Villarreal so there are stiff tests to come.

Sporting are well-placed after three wins from four, but their Champions League schedule is rather one-sided: in their final three matches they travel to Roma, before playing Barcelona and Manchester City. They reached the quarter-finals of the competition last season, losing narrowly to Arsenal over two legs.

They are third in their league, having been weakened by the summer sales of Geovany Quenda (to Chelsea), Morten Hjulmand (to Atletico Madrid) and Ousmane Diomande (to Nottingham Forest). The vast majority of goals are scored by Colombian striker Luis Suárez.

Bruno Fernandes, United’s captain, returns to his former club tonight and there is hope Luke Shaw could be back at left-back. Pochettino must decide whether or not to stick with Matthijs de Ligt, who was extremely rusty at Anfield but may need the minutes.

Yoro’s one-game suspension was overturned by the FA, and he would have been available for this one in any case.

#927. Inside the mind games that will decide Arsenal v Man City

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mikel Arteta was punished by Pep Guardiola after a crucial selection in the Carabao Cup final, now, Miguel Delaney writes, he holds the experience and power to land a decisive blow on their bitter title rivals

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Manchester City have a lot of bigger concerns right now but some of Enzo Maresca’s staff have naturally been conscious of the noise around David Raya. The goalkeeper was not wearing a sling at Tuesday’s Champions League match against Borussia Dortmund, after he had so conspicuously been photographed sporting one on London’s busiest street just two days before.

It’s certainly true the injury suffered at Newcastle United is nowhere near as bad as first feared, with contact on a nerve having apparently caused the initial issue.

Some on the City side have wondered whether Mikel Arteta is using it to play his usual games. The manager likes to use media and even official squad photos to keep opposition guessing.

It would be especially understandable here, since this position could go a long way to deciding Sunday’s game.

The entire decision on Raya, in fact, draws out so many of its strands and storylines.

Both sides are especially attuned to it since it was as recently as March's Carabao Cup final that Pep Guardiola’s response to the Kepa Arrizabalaga selection essentially decided that game.

It might even have been the Catalan’s last piece of genius in England. Arsenal couldn’t play out of the press without Raya's passing, and City gradually shut them down. The tactical effect of it was so pronounced that it framed the thinking of both clubs ahead of April’s suffocatingly tense Premier League showdown.

That 2-1 City win might well go down as one of those influential defeats, rather than decisive victories, because of the effect on Arsenal. They actually gleaned confidence and instruction, to win all of their remaining games.

And now they're champions, and intent on asserting exactly what that means - with Raya's injury currently the primary concern.

Except, aside from it looking 50-50 over whether Raya will be involved, Guardiola certainly won’t be. The man responsible for that tactical thinking isn't there. And even if there is now debate over Maresca’s exact quality as a coach, he’s not Guardiola.

The dysfunction of his own pressing system, and City’s newly profound susceptibility to counter-attacks, also means they may not be able to execute any such approach in the same way… but then very little about City is the same.

The very consequence of this match might even change.

It all adds to the feel of this being a defining game for this most peculiar of seasons.

Arsenal can win to emphatically kill City’s title challenge… but will that even be a title challenge? City can win to transform the entire dynamic around the top of the table, but will the outcome of their appeal skew it in a way the Premier League has never seen?

Or, what if they win and then win their appeal - however unlikely legal figures currently think that is - to then go on a run?

It’s an absurd context, and that for a fixture that has recently been freighted with greater meaning.

And it is because of that recent history that Arsenal do feel they owe City one.

Arteta is said to feel it was absolutely crucial they won the title before Guardiola left and the verdict of the long-running Premier League case came in.

It was about proving it on their own terms. And now, with City precarious, they want to fully prove their superiority; to emphasise this can be their era; to put City out of the picture.

Despite enduring two comebacks for draws in their last two matches, the Arsenal squad are in a good mood.

They feel they played excellently for 160 minutes of those games and that just continuing that will have them in good stead over an awkward run of fixtures.

Or, as one figure told the Independent: “We are due to hammer someone”.

And, as another said separately: “We need to hammer City on Sunday”.

Everyone at Arsenal knows that is much easier said than done.

Despite all of City’s recent problems, the rivalry of this fixture might just be the type of game Maresca’s side require. It might cause them to dig deep.

That of course may depend on how deep their problems actually are.

One recent argument coming out of City has been that this is all just tactical, and individual moments in individual games are going against them.

It’s just that the idea this slump is solely down to tactical/technical issues feels… a stretch.

Really, City are in a situation of remarkable extremes.

Even the departure of Guardiola would have been enough to distort an entire season. If City are obviously better structured than Manchester United after Sir Alex Ferguson or Arsenal themselves after Arsene Wenger, it is still adapting to the absence of one of the most psychologically imposing figures in football. His presence was immense.

That alone creates a vacuum, that is arguably manifesting in City's dysfunctional midfield.

That area also poses significant tactical questions about Guardiola's successor. Insiders familiar with both Chelsea and Leicester City can’t help notice familiar flaws in Maresca’s teams, especially as regards the balance. City are just so easy to get at.

You can even map previous Chelsea form onto this season. Maresca’s first season at Stamford Bridge in 2024-25 started well, to the point of being talked of as title challengers, only to endure a winter drop-off surrounded by the same tactical discussions.

The City squad are going through a situation no one in English football history has ever experienced. You can even extend that to European football, despite various controversies, given how long this entire process has been.

Another line from inside the club is that they are as adamant with the players as they are with everyone else: that they will overturn this verdict, and big questions will instead be posted to the rest of the Premier League.

Some at rival clubs even think that one element of City’s belligerent response, at least in public, has been as a message to the players.

They need to radiate a sense of business as usual so as to convince the squad, because they do need the actual football business to indeed be as it usually is. They know they need to keep them focused.

That’s just very difficult to do when the potential consequences could come this season, which recent results arguably show.

Because, even if the players themselves honestly insist they are genuinely fully focused, this is still a story that has major implications for their careers. They may have to take big decisions. Some might even be thinking this is a waste of a season in a short career.

That is going to at least have some effect, even if it is subconscious.

It creates a cloud of doubt, and this in a sport that demands more intensity of focus than ever before. The opposition manager, Arteta, demands it more than anyone else. Guardiola himself was a huge influence in this.

Both have abruptly discarded numerous players if they sensed that a necessary tunnel vision had been obscured by even 1 per cent.

And that is exactly what a situation like this does. It's too big to just completely shut out.

Without it, City might have even been better able to work around some of the tactical issues.

In short, even if performances have been OK, this does not look like a team playing to optimum level.

Neither do Arsenal but they don’t feel too far off. They're primed. City might well need that challenge to rouse themselves.

Either way, it is already a fixture that feels like it has the makings of a huge result. And also a result that might mean absolutely nothing by the end.
