#926. The biggest fear behind the Premier League’s controversial move to digital football tickets

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The Premier League’s decision to fully introduce digital tickets this campaign has sparked a ‘secret civil war’, writes Miguel Delaney, with fans increasingly concerned that the season ticket could be about to disappear for good - with significant consequences

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

It is described as the Premier League’s “secret civil war”, except it’s very public. So much so that it affects the majority of those who fill stadiums every single week. It affects the lifeblood of football… but then the entire point is that this isn’t something tangible you can touch.

This season’s full introduction of digital tickets has affected fan behaviour and community.

You can see it in queues outside games. You can hear it in discussions on the difficulty of “passing on” tickets, and arguably even atmosphere.

Duncan Drasdo of the Manchester United Supporters Trust says, “it absolutely impacts fan culture”.

The Football Supporters’ Association say they are “monitoring” how it progresses but it all plays into a deeper sense, that there is a long-term aim to eventually end season tickets altogether.

Multiple clubs contacted for this article strenuously dispute this, and many are quite strident on their position.

The move comes from a vote in the summer of 2024, where there was effusive support for the mandatory introduction of digital tickets from the start of this season. This essentially means doing away with old physical tickets - although clubs can still give them out in special cases - for ones now scanned. And, if holders can’t go, they can pass to selected family and friends, or put on the club exchange.

There are two primary arguments the clubs make. One is cutting down on touting, which they insist is still absolutely rife. Club sources say the data showed networks where people were running 50-60 season-ticket accounts, and there was financial gain. They argue that runs contrary to the idea of the season ticket being personal to a fan for their loyalty, and insist the only action - achieved through hidden barcodes - is against abuse.

The other is increasing safety, and knowing everyone who is in the stadium. It inherently conditions better behaviour, since anyone can be tracked.

Fan groups accept parts of these arguments, and would acknowledge that a lot of their clubs directly engage, but sympathy has been eroded by direct experience. Almost immediately, there were long queues outside games, many of which have lingered. Most pertinently, though, there is the sudden negating of what has long been normal. Every season-ticket holder will know it, as will those who use their tickets. “Passing on” is a lot more difficult, as clubs increase obligation for the ticket to be used in some form.

“And passing it on is absolutely fan culture,” says Gareth Roberts, of Liverpool’s Spirit of Shankly group. Drasdo adds: “It’s what creates community.”

A common complaint is that it now involves more laborious processes, and doing it unofficially potentially risks a ban, when you used to be able to just hand it to someone.

“Not just talking about Liverpool here, but I do know of fans who do get worried about it,” Roberts says. “There are so many rules and regulations to take in, it’s almost like taking an exam. It feels a heavy load to be a supporter.

“Through not filling in the initial form as they wanted, I have one mate who can’t go to Champions League games and two who can’t go to cups. The assumption is that everyone is digitally literate, but they don’t.”

This has practical concerns, too, if a fan can’t go at short notice.

“We’ve been saying there should be ways to do this,” Roberts says. “You’re not setting up a business and earning from this. OK, there are touts but they have to think of ways to not impinge on traditional fans.”

Darren Epstein, a Gold Rep at Arsenal, says the complication of it all is under-appreciated: “In days gone by, we’d be talking about managers and tactics. Now it’s when away tickets go on sale, collections, ID checks, and points - points being the loyalty points you get on buying an away ticket.

“It feels like a constant battle to ensure you get to a game. Although, changes have undoubtedly improved the ability of many fans to get to games they never have been able to before, which many of course feel is a good thing.”

A connected complaint is that this is one more factor affecting traditional atmospheres.

“If it’s the club re-selling the ticket on the exchange, it changes the profile of the support, introducing a random fan into a group of mates,” Drasdo says. “In the old standing sections you were able to congregate with friends but the introduction of all-seater stadia meant people got split up by where their seats were and we lost that mobility which is the key to atmosphere."

Tom Concannon of the FSA, speaking as a Newcastle United fan, says: “Atmospheres are worsening because of it in my opinion. Tickets are going to those wanting to experience the atmosphere rather than contribute to it.” Roberts adds: “Atmosphere is dependent on youth vibrancy. The Kop is pretty old now.”

Even in simple terms, it’s a lot harder to pass on tickets to children who may not have a phone, but that clubs actively need to get that match-day buzz. Fan representatives would similarly say it doesn’t help that the Premier League’s clubs’ ticketing working group only has heads of ticketing on it, rather than actual match-going fans.

Such concern feeds into a deeper tension in all of this, between being a supporter and being a customer. An irony is that it means fans have less control over what they pay for. As one executive says, “if you’ve bought your season ticket, you should have no obligation to sit in the seat”.

Another perspective is that clubs are being more strict and trying to get control of every ticket they can. One industry figure points to how the same data from digital tickets has allowed clubs to see just how often tickets are passed on, and it has stunned them. One club has estimated that 20-25 per cent of tickets are passed on, which they also see as running contrary to what a season ticket is supposed to be.

Or, as some fans put, they realised they could monetise. Tickets not passed on can be put on the ticket exchange, where FSA research shows prices are considerably higher than the average for a season-ticket seat.

Club sources would say they deliberately decoupled the season-ticket price from match-by-match, to recognise the value of a season-ticket holder.

Drasdo offers a different view: “A common phrase we hear from our fans is ‘the club are the biggest touts of all’, which is essentially a reaction to the restrictions on usage and the premium prices we see when season ticket holders' tickets are resold by the club.

“A major problem we’ve had at United is stretching the gap in price between season ticket holders and member ticket prices which causes the club to focus on how season ticket holders pass on their tickets when not personally attending.”

Another knock-on has been what Roberts describes as the “normalisation” of fans who don’t have season tickets paying fees to become members to go into lotteries for tickets. Some clubs even charge for transferring. Most clubs have unlimited membership, meaning there is actually less chance of getting a ticket.

“We’ll never really know how many tickets end up in the hands of actual fans,” Concannon says. “Hospitality numbers are on the rise.”

Clubs would nevertheless insist they are acutely conscious of this, and they have to allow opportunities for fans on long waiting lists, or who otherwise feel shut out of being able to go to games. That has fostered tension between supporters, as well as between supporters and clubs. Fans who speak out often find themselves shouted down by others who say “if you don’t pay it, I will”.

And yet such demand comes at a different cost, as anecdotal evidence suggests a lot of long-time supporters are being worn down. “There’s an underbelly of that growing, that clubs don’t realise,” Roberts argues. “If you’re constantly made to jump through these hoops.”

Such weariness has even been deepened by two other concerns. One is this long-time fear that clubs actually want to get rid of season tickets, so they can sell more seats for higher prices. Club sources are adamant that is not the case, as illustrated by how season tickets stripped from some fans are redistributed to those on the waiting list. Whether that is true or not, a step like this could serve as a halfway step for the future.

Clubs themselves would point to escalating player costs and fans wanting the best possible team on the pitch but, as with redundancies, this is dismissed. “A nonsense notion,” Concannon says, “£25 from every fan at every Premier League game only just paid the agents’ bills last season.”

One chief executive actually links the entire issue to the financial rules. “The point of forcing bums on seats should be atmosphere,” they say. “The ugly extra money-making for clubs is not on. Clubs do need protection - if they had cost-control protection they would not be fleecing fans.”

Some clubs would accept there could have been better communication. For now, if you go to a game this weekend, it’s what a lot of fans are talking about.

Newcastle United and head coach Matthias Jaissle could reunite with a former striker, according to reports

Newcastle are being tipped to solve their goalscoring issues this winter with a move to bring Ivan Toney back to St James’ Park.

It is a transfer which would reunite the England international with former boss Matthias Jaissle, with whom he worked at current club Al-Ahli.

Finding the back of the net has proved a major headache for Jaissle since taking the reins on Tyneside and following a summer exodus that stripped the Magpies of their spine, none of Newcastle’s current central striking options have managed to nail down a starting spot in his team.

Will Osula and Yoane Wissa have mustered just a single league goal apiece so far this campaign, while Matias Fernandez-Pardo is still waiting to open his account. Without a reliable penalty-box presence, Jaissle’s side have lacked a cutting edge in the final third.

Toney thrived under Jaissle during their time together in Saudi Arabia. The former Brentford frontman has been expectedly prolific in the Middle East, netting 87 times in 110 appearances across all competitions.

Any transfer negotiations may even be smoothed over by shared ownership links, as both Al-Ahli and Newcastle are majority-owned by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

Despite his form in the Saudi Pro League, Toney has slipped down the international pecking order and missed out on recent England squads, a setback that is expected to spark a push for a Premier League return in the New Year.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Speaking on the Everything is Black and White Podcast, The Chronicle’s chief Newcastle reporter Lee Ryder suggested the 30-year-old will be chomping at the bit to head back to English football.

A switch to St James’ Park would see Toney return to the club he departed almost a decade ago. Newcastle originally signed the striker from Northampton Town over in 2015, but made just two Premier League outings before being sent out on a series of loans. Spells at Barnsley, Shrewsbury, Scunthorpe and Wigan followed, before he was eventually sold to Peterborough United in 2018.

Having since proved his top-flight pedigree at Brentford, Toney would bring additional physicality and an aptitude for finishing that Newcastle are presently missing.

#924. Germany news: Plans for Rwanda migrant hub come under fire

Human rights groups have slammed plans by Germany and four other EU states to send rejected asylum seekers to Rwanda. In other news, business start-ups in Germany are on track to reach the highest level since 2015.

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, November 17, 2026:

We'll be back with the latest headlines out of Germany tomorrow, thank you for staying with us. Tschüss!

German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius backed Ukraine in the aftermath of the Crimea bridge strike.

Pistorius said ‌criticism of ​Ukraine's deep strikes in ​Russia was ​misplaced.

In particular, Pistorius responded to US Defense Under Secretary Elbridge Colby, who said Ukraine's "deep strikes" against Russia "have not been effective in driving an end to the war."

The German defense minister said "criticizing strikes like that in Russia to destroy strategic military and military-used targets" was "quite a ​stupid thing."

"Instead ‌of criticizing that, we should rather criticize and talk about the terroristic strikes every night and every day on... energy, water, and heating infrastructure in Ukraine. This is kind of terrorism," Pistorius said.

He added that attacks inside ⁠Russia ​against ​non-civilian targets ​and sites used ‌by the military ​are ⁠legal and legitimate targets.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Former US President Joe Biden's new autobiography "Promise Me, America" hit bookshelves on Tuesday, and it features anecdotes about several global leaders, including former German Chancellor Angela Merkel.

In the book, Biden dished on conversations that he and Merkel had about his predecessor and later successor, Donald Trump.

Citing conversations from early 2021, Biden wrote, "Angela was candid about her frustrations with my predecessor, who refused to shake her hand, and who seemed 'emotional' in their meetings, driven by mood swings rather than facts."

"She also wondered," wrote Biden, "why he was 'fascinated' by Vladimir Putin and other politicians 'with autocratic and dictatorial traits.' That was a mystery I could not unravel."

Merkel and Trump were often at odds over issues tied to NATO, trade, climate policy and Germany's dependence on Russian energy but one of the most infamous meetings between two came in the Oval Office in March 2017, when Trump awkwardly refused to shake hands with the German leader during a press availability despite photographers loudly encouraging him to do so.

Merkel reflected on the moment in her own 2024 memoir "Freedom" saying that after initially approaching Trump as someone "completely normal" she quickly sensed that he viewed their public meetings as a kind of "you or me" competition.

The UN's high commissioner for human rights, Volker Türk, has joined the chorus of those voicing doubts about a plan by five EU countries, including Germany, to send rejected asylum seekers ​to a deportation hub ​in ‌Rwanda.

Türk said he had not yet ‌seen the draft proposal ‌but that ​his office was "concerned about the human rights risks raised by ​the proposed transfer of people from five ⁠European Union ​countries to ​Rwanda, where they have no ​genuine connection and ‌which has its own set ​of ⁠human rights challenges."

Instead, he called ⁠for ​a "comprehensive approach to migration governance anchored in human rights."

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck" (see entry below).

New figures from the EU statistics agency show that just over one quarter of all students from abroad in various EU member states were enrolled in tertiary education in Germany.

Of a total of roughly 1.65 million foreign students in 2024, around 1.1 million of them were from outside the EU and the rest were moving within the EU, 438,260 were in Germany.

France was next in line by sheer numbers with almost 285,000 foreign students, and the much less populous Netherlands was third with over 176,000. Germany, France and the Netherlands combined accounted for more than half the bloc-wide total.

The Netherlands, unlike France and Germany, was also one of the countries with the highest proportion of foreign students in tertiary education. Even excluding doctoral-level students, around 18% of students in the Netherlands hailed from abroad.

Only Luxembourg, at 51.5%, Malta (35.6%), Cyprus (21.6%) and Austria (20.8%)  had a higher share among full EU members, though Switzerland's ratio also stood at roughly 20%.

Greece (2.6%), Croatia (3.5%) and Spain (4.6'%) had some of the lowest percentages of foreign students, with the EU average at 8.7%.

Mediation between German flagship carrier Lufthansa and the Vereinigung Cockpit (VC) pilots' trade union ended on Tuesday without a clear breakthrough.

The airline is trying to cut costs while the union is trying to optimize pay and conditions for members in a dispute dating back to September 2025 that led to several disruptions earlier in the year.

VC said that it favored a package resulting from the mediation, which it said Lufthansa had rejected. VC said it was giving the airline until November 23 to reconsider its position.

"The ball is now in the employer's court," VC said in a call with media. It did not specify what action it would take after the deadline but did say it considered its commitment not to strike during the arbitration process to be satisfied.

Lufthansa, meanwhile, said it had submitted a proposal to VC for up to 1,000 new cockpit hires by 2033, up to 150 additional captain promotions each year, a one-off payment for 2027 and 2028 followed by salary increases from 2029 onwards.

VC said it would be willing to make further concessions on pay and conditions if Lufthansa would respond with job guarantees.

The airline also said arbitrators had indicated a willingness to continue negotiations if the latest round proved fruitless — though it wasn't clear whether that also applied to each side of the labor dispute.

The government of the city-state of Berlin has banned an association accused of supporting the Lebanese group Hezbollah, which has been deemed a terrorist organization and outlawed in Germany since 2020.

Police in Berlin searched a total of 28 properties on Tuesday, including premises belonging to the affected groups and the homes of select members.

The ban affects El-Irschad e.V. in the Neukölln district and three subsidiary groups: Al-Qaem e.V., Al-Thaqalyn e.V., and Qalam Bildungszentrum UG.

The city's senator, or Cabinet minister, for interior affairs, Iris Spranger of the Social Democrats, said the group was "directed against the notions of understanding between peoples," and that its "purpose and activities" contravened criminal laws in Berlin.

The ban prohibits the public display or distribution of the organizations' symbols and logos. Their websites have been shut down and their assets seized.

Spranger said the group had given Hezbollah a platform to spread propaganda among Neukölln's Shiite community, using youth activities and a mosque to do so.

A number of human rights groups have spoken out after Germany, along with Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands, announced plans to set up a hub for rejected migrants in Rwanda.

The deportation center would be the first such facility outside the European Union.

The Germany-based refugee advocacy group Pro Asyl said on Tuesday that the plans would end in a "shipwreck."

Pro Asyl managing director Karl Kopp said that even rejected asylum seekers had rights.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition figures there are arrested and sometimes tortured," he said.

"If those affected need help, we will stand at their side with legal support."

In a statement issued after the announcement of the plans, 45 NGOs from 15 countries also condemned the move.

"These plans allow people without a right to stay in the EU to be sent to countries with which they have no connection at all," the statement said.

"These policies shift people, and responsibility for their safety and rights, out of public sight and beyond scrutiny," it said.

The junior partner in Germany's coalition, the center-left Social Democrats, has also maintained its criticism of the plans, which are heavily supported by Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt of the Bavarian Christian Social Union (CSU), the sister party of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's Christian Democrats (CDU).

"Dobrindt's plans are short-sighted with regard to foreign policy and harm Germany's credibility," SPD foreign policy spokesman Adid Ahmetovic told the Reuters news agency.

"Rwanda violates the sovereignty of its neighbors and supports the M23 rebels in eastern [Democratic Republic of] Congo," he said.

"Such a regime must not receive any political concessions just because it is to take in refugees from Germany," he said, adding: "Human rights are not bargaining chips for deportation deals."

The announcement of the plans comes after an EU reform of its migration policy this year granted broader detention powers and allowed for the creation of return hubs.

According to Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker, the aim is for the first center to be set up in Rwanda next year.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot with some 100 people, 20 from each of the five nations.

The plan to establish the deportation center in Rwanda has drawn criticism not only from a wide range of human rights groups but also from the junior partner in Germany's ruling coalition, the Social Democrats (SPD), as this video details.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Germany will be purchasing $300 million (€273 million) of US arms supplies to give to Ukraine as it fights against the Russian invasion,  German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on Tuesday.

He said that Berlin was making a fifth contribution to the PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism coordinated by the US and NATO, under which European countries finance the purchase of US weapons for Ukraine.

Most of the new funds will go to buy guided missiles for Patriot air defense systems, Pistorius said in remarks made on the sidelines of a meeting with his EU counterparts in Brussels.

He said Berlin was also planning to provide Kyiv with IRIS-T air defense systems, as previously announced, as well as new radars to improve air surveillance, ammunition for F-16 fighter jets, and drones.

He also said that Germany was preparing to make IRIS-T missiles compatible with NASAMS air defense systems being supplied to Ukraine by Norway.

Pistorius stressed that supporting Ukraine, although an act of solidarity, was "not a charity event," as Russian aggression posed an associated threat to Western Europe.

He is to host a meeting alongside his British counterpart Wes Streeting later on Tuesday that aims to drum up further military support for Kyiv.

Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul has said he would like Germany to expand its relations with the former Soviet republics of Azerbaijan and Armenia as a counterweight to an ongoing bid by Russia to maintain its influence in the region.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence at the expense of the people and their future," Wadephul on Tuesday before setting off on his first visit to the two countries as foreign minister.

He said Russian President Vladimir Putin was opposed to countries deciding their own destiny under a European order of sovereign states, making it important for the two Caucasian nations to retain their self-determination over their futures.

Wadephul also highlighted the South Caucasus's role as an interface between Europe and Asia, which he said meant the region had great potential for trade, energy partnerships and new transport links.

Germany's top diplomat is first to visit the Azerbaijani capital, Baku, where he is set to meet the country's authoritarian head of state, Ilham Aliyev, and Foreign Minister Ceyhun Bayramov.

He is scheduled to travel on to Armenia on Wednesday.

In August 2025, the two countries signed a joint declaration on a US-brokered peace treaty ending a decadeslong conflict over the Nagorno-Karabakh region.

This came after Azerbaijan captured the region in 2023 in a short but heavy offensive, with most of the region's population — more than 100,000 ethnic Armenians — forced to flee.

Shares in Deutsche Bank took a nosedive on Tuesday after media across the world published reports with information gleaned from millions of leaked documents that expose dubious past business practices at the lender.

The documents, which were shared by unidentified whistleblowers, throw light on the banking giant's activities over the past 20 years, which include dealings with Russian oligarchs and the late convicted US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

The name Donald Trump also appears in the documents from the time before he became US president.

The leaked documents, which include emails, have cast doubt on the success of chief executive Christian Sewing's efforts to turn around the institution after a series of scandals.

Among other things, they indicate that Sewing himself was involved in a working group that  sought to expand the bank's Russian operations shortly before Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, despite warnings about regulatory and money-laundering risks.

The investigation, called "Inside Deutsche Bank", was conducted by over 200 journalists from a media consortium that included The Financial Times, Der Spiegel, Le Monde, the New York Times, the German public broadcaster ZDF and the Austrian daily Der Standard.

Deutsche Bank has not disputed the authenticity of the data, though it refers to the documents as "purported internal documents."

It also said that many of the incidents referred to in them belonged to a distant past and that it is now "a different bank."

The European Commission has almost doubled its forecast for economic growth in Germany, raising it from a prediction in spring of 0.6% to 1.3% now.

The commission said stable domestic consumer demand and a rebound in exports justified the more optimistic figure.

The higher forecast comes despite the high inflation rate caused by the war in Iran.

Some 286,000 new businesses are expected to be founded in 2026, a rise of 3.4% compared with last year and the highest level of start-ups since 2015, according to the National Association of German Cooperative Banks (BVR).

The BVR said the boom in start-ups could be partly attributed to the fact that developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and a difficult situation on the labor market were making self-employment more profitable.

However, the association warned that the increase was fragile, as it was largely driven by government support and exports rather that the private investment needed for more sustained growth.

In July, the German government adopted a start-up strategy that aimed to cut bureaucracy and provide support for future technologies, thus creating favorable conditions for young entrepreneurs.

The BVR also cautioned that the number of people in the 30-40 age group — those most likely to start a business — was falling, meaning that the surge will probably not last.

The association also said that even though there was a rise in AI-related start-ups in 2026, Europe needed to do more for AI development to keep up with the US and China.

DW's newsroom on the Rhine in Bonn wishes all readers a guten Tag!

Plans announced by Germany and four EU partner states to deport rejected asylum seekers to a hub in Rwanda have provoked a wave of criticism from human rights groups.

Migration hard-liner Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt, one of the main advocates of the plan, has, however, given assurances that it will be executed "in line with human rights" and "in accordance with European and German law."

Meanwhile, more new businesses are expected to open in Germany this year than has been the case since 2015, a rise partly driven by the growing presence of artificial intelligence.

And internal documents leaked by whistleblowers from Deutsche Bank, a lender that has had more than its fair share of scandals in the past, have exposed more cases of malpractice and misconduct in recent years, media say.

#923. The world’s leading science cities are changing — here’s why

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Aerial scenery of Hengqin Free Trade Zone, China. Credit: Weiming Xie/Shutterstock

Two-thirds of the world’s population will be living in cities by 2050, according to the latest estimates by the United Nations. Coinciding with the mass movement of people into urban areas is the rapid integration of technology into many of those spaces. From automated subterranean waste-collection systems to driverless vehicle zones, these ‘smart-city’ solutions are changing the way that people live, work and move through their environments.

Some cities are embracing these technological advances at a much faster pace than others. Places such as Beijing, Helsinki, London and Singapore stand out for the way they are integrating smart-city technology into existing infrastructure and services.

Other cities are emerging with these technologies integral to their operations from their inception. But as the examples of Songdo in South Korea and Hengqin in China illustrate, building smart infrastructure from scratch is only half the challenge: these places must also attract and retain the research and innovation talent needed to develop, operate and improve it. It’s a ‘chicken-and-egg’ problem, says Songdo-based urban-planning researcher, Dakota McCarty: talent follows world-class universities and thriving economic zones, which need a critical mass of expertise and investment to be attractive.

#922. Ten-man Bournemouth battle back to score Europa League victory at Celta Vigo

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Celta Vigo 1-2 Bournemouth: The Cherries lost Bafode Diakite to a 23rd-minute red card but battled back from going a goal behind to win in Spain

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Bournemouth moved a step closer to automatic qualification for the Europa League last 16 after coming from behind with 10 men to win 2-1 at Celta Vigo.

It was a remarkable 10th victory in a row in all competitions for Marco Rose’s side and it might have been the most satisfying of the lot for the manager, coming as it did after his team had found themselves a goal down and a man down at half-time.

The visitors looked in trouble when, minutes after Iago Aspas had curled Celta in front, Bafode Diakite was red-carded for a poorly timed tackle.

Bournemouth might have folded then, but instead they came roaring back, Alvaro Rodriguez heading them level almost immediately after the start of the second half.

A draw would have been an excellent result in the circumstances. Substitute Rayan had other ideas, waiting at the end of a rapid breakaway to sweep in the winner 12 minutes from time.

Victory against Viktoria Plzen in December will almost certainly now be enough to earn direct passage to the last 16.

Pablo Duran had the ball in the Bournemouth net after 10 minutes after it spilled back to him off Michele Di Gregorio, the goalkeeper relieved to see the offside flag go up against the Celta striker.

The stand-in keeper redeemed himself minutes later with a solid save from an outrageous bicycle kick by Aspas. It would have been a remarkable goal but the Celta great would not be denied. Bournemouth failed fully to get the ball away, and from the edge of the box Aspas curled a beauty in off the far post.

Bournemouth had gone behind in the first half of their last game in this competition at Sparta Prague. That night, the balance was tipped almost immediately in their favour by a red card for the Czech side, but here it was Rose’s team who found themselves down to 10 men.

Diakite made an honest attempt to win the ball but was late and his studs landed on the ankle of Couhaib Driouech. An initial yellow card was overturned following a VAR check and Bournemouth were on the ropes.

It had been the most challenging half of their debut European campaign, but within minutes of the start of the second period, they were level.

Amine Adli was left in space outside the box to send over a wonderful cross to the far post. Arriving there was Rodriguez, sneaking ahead of his defender to get a head on the ball and nod in the equaliser.

A wonderful counter-attack brought the Premier League side their winner. Adrien Truffert showed good strength out on left to outmuscle Sergio Carreira, and he fed the ball up to Marcus Tavernier. He might have shot himself but instead moved it on to Rayan who swept home.

#920. Could the Airbus €3 billion loan row reignite a US-EU trade dispute?

The US says a record €3 billion financing package for Airbus may conflict with a transatlantic aircraft-subsidy truce. EU officials insist the funding complies with market-based rules.

A fresh row over a record-breaking EU loan to European aerospace company Airbus could reopen a long-standing rift with Washington and threaten an existing EU-US trade truce.

The European Investment Bank (EIB), the lending arm of the EU, agreed in June to loan Airbus up to €3 billion ($3.4 billion) but US President Donald Trump's top trade advisor recently suggested the loan breached a 2021 EU-US agreement on state support.

"I had sincerely hoped that trade-distorting European subsidies to Airbus were a thing of the past," US Trade Representative Jamieson Grier said in late October. "For decades, France, Germany and Spain have aggressively supported Airbus, their national champion aircraft manufacturer, to gain an unfair advantage over US aerospace workers and business."

He also suggested there was a lack of transparency around the terms of the loan. The EU insists the loan does not amount to subsidies, that it is in close contact with the Office of the US Trade Representative and "will provide all necessary information," a spokesperson told DW.

An Airbus spokesperson told DW the company is "actively engaging with the relevant authorities and are happy to share more information about the loan with governments."

Airbus and the US company Boeing, the world's two largest plane manufacturers, were previously involved in a 17-year corporate trade dispute.

The World Trade Organization (WTO) ruled that both the EU and US provided the companies with state subsidies, resulting in years of tariffs, tit-for-tat retaliation and claims of victory by both sides.

A deal to end tariffs with strict provisions on state support was finally agreed in 2021 and strengthened in 2025, but the latest row threatens to reopen the dispute and could potentially threaten the wider EU-US tariff deal agreed last year, experts say.

The previous Airbus-Boeing dispute was one of the longest-running corporate disputes in history and led to billions of dollars' worth of tariffs leveled by both sides.

"Trade experts tend to hate to talk about it because there are so many ups and downs to the story, it took so long to get resolved and it always tends to creep back up again," Inu Manak, a senior fellow at the Peterson Institute for International Economics who specializes in international trade law and policy, told DW.

She says because the issue is such a "persistent thorn in the side," it has the potential to spiral, but for now the US is only signaling displeasure before things escalate. "They want to talk about this, and that conversation will need to happen before anything goes further," she said.

At the heart of the current dispute is whether the €3 billion loan from the EIB, the largest corporate loan ever authorized by the bank, amounts to illegal state support.

"The EIB loan to Airbus is a standard loan on market terms," a European Commission spokesperson told DW. "It carries interest, it must be repaid in full, and it is the type of financing the EIB provides every year to companies across many sectors."

A spokesperson for the bank told DW the €3 billion loan is "a standard EIB corporate loan, implemented under the bank's established procedures and on market-based terms." It says it considers the financing to be "fully consistent with the market-terms principle" of the 2021 deal.

A spokesperson for Airbus told DW the loan is "a standard corporate financing facility, similar to commercially available loans we've signed in the past."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Fredrik Erixon, founding director of the European Center for International Political Economy, says the lines are still blurred when it comes to what counts as a subsidy and what is just a loan and that only a comprehensive World Trade Organization investigation could establish the full facts.

Another potential issue is how the €3 billion will be used, including the share earmarked for research and development and how much funding will support defense-related activities versus commercial aircraft development.

Inu Manak says it is impossible at this point to determine if the loan amounts to the provision of illegal subsidies or not, and that it depends on the very specific terms of the credit provided and whether or not it could be proved to be damaging to Boeing's business.

"If it's a market-based loan, if it's not providing below-market rates that would provide an unfair advantage, then it should be fine," she said. "That remains to be seen."

In Erixon's view, the situation is further complicated by the fact that the aerospace sector is "a highly murky business" due to the amount of defense contracts companies like Boeing and Airbus hold with governments and the high costs associated with that in terms of research and development.

"The problem is we've ended up in a world where there's only two large aircraft manufacturers," he told DW. "And it is a business with high upfront costs when you're going to develop different things."

He points out that while Boeing may have a legitimate grievance over this loan, Airbus and the EU can point to Boeing's own deals with the US government.

"Boeing does R&D contracts for military purposes, which end up producing technology and support for the civil aircraft program for Boeing," said Erixon. "That's also what the World Trade Organization found previously."

It was Boeing that originally asked the US trade representative back in July to intervene over the loan, linking it to Airbus' plan to develop a new single-aisle aircraft program, which could spark a new era of intense competition between the two giants. Neither the US trade representative nor Boeing responded to a DW request for comment.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Inu Manak thinks the next obvious step for the US would be to launch a Section 301 investigation, which is an official inquiry to determine if the loan "violates an international trade agreement or is unjustified, unreasonable or discriminatory, and that burdens or restricts US commerce."

She thinks the Trump administration has no interest in engaging with the WTO and believes it has the potential to threaten the broader EU-US trade agreement.

"I don't think there's a lot that can stop the US trade representative from taking action if they decide they want to do it," Manak said. "They may think there may be something else to extract from the European Union."

Fredrik Erixon agrees that "it's going to be a point of leverage that the Americans can use against Europe," adding that the dynamics underpinning the aerospace sector — that both Boeing and Airbus need greater government investment due to ramped-up military spending — is the fundamental underlying problem.

"We are getting into a state aid race, which basically means these companies just need more and more and more money," he said. "That in itself is an escalatory development."

Thomas Frank secured his first win as Crystal Palace boss but admitted his new side nearly nearly gave him a “heart attack” in the nervy final five minutes of their 2-1 Europa League comeback against 10-man Real Sociedad.

Chelsea loanee Mamadou Sarr broke the deadlock for the visitors in the 66th minute at Selhurst Park but Frank’s first home contest turned on its head when Jon Martin received a second yellow card six minutes later.

Jean-Philippe Mateta drew the sides level from the penalty spot and Dwight McNeil poked Palace into the lead from fellow substitute Jorgen Strand Larsen’s bicycle kick, but they were denied a chance to put the game away when Yeremy Pino’s penalty was saved.

“I think first and foremost to get it over the line, and (it was) an extremely important win for various reasons,” said Frank, who took charge of Premier League basement club Palace for the first time in Saturday’s league loss to Coventry.

“One, of course, confidence, and it relates to belief against an extremely good team. I think the first half we were compact and very disciplined in many ways. We missed the high-pressure situations we had, and I think we struggled to keep the ball well enough.

“Second half I felt we were much better in the high pressure, and I felt we kept the ball much better. I actually felt we got a bit more momentum in the second half but then, out of the blue, they scored the 1-0 goal.

“But what I really like is the belief from the players, what they showed, and that we are threatening on set-pieces, we cannot underestimate that.”

Unai Marrero’s save to deny Pino from the spot kept the Spanish side in with a chance of an equaliser and it nearly came at the death from Orri Oskarsson, whose effort was pushed away by Dean Henderson – his last of six saves on Thursday night.

“We know in football one moment can change the game,” Frank continued. “The penalty and the red card changed the game, then we still needed to score.

“To win still is important and we went brave, we went with the offensive substitutions and kept two strikers on the pitch, and that paid off.

“And then I think we were all close to getting a heart attack in the last five minutes.”

Frank agreed the win could be a significant turning point for Palace’s fortunes ahead of a critical Premier League clash with Hull on Sunday.

“That’s why it’s so important to keep doing the right things, keep believing, and keep going,” he said.

Palace’s Premier League survival remains the priority but the result also propelled the Eagles into play-off position in their European campaign, four places out of the top eight after five matches.

Asked about his ambitions for the European campaign – given Palace’s league position – Frank replied: “I think we want to aim high.

“We are ambitious for this tournament, and that’s why the win was so important.”

#917. Alonso crisis deepens as chaotic Chelsea lose and fans taunt own player

It always feels like Chelsea are not far away from a crisis and Xabi Alonso has now lost more Premier League games this season than Manchester United.

Alonso will inevitably come under further scrutiny after another alarming result and performance, with unpopular centre-back Wesley Fofana also targeted by Chelsea’s supporters.

Chants of “f--- off Fofana, you’re not wanted here” were clearly heard from the away end after another excruciating experience for the defender.

After an ill-advised interview earlier this week, Fofana followed that up with a string of mistakes which led to Nottingham Forest’s second goal.

Forest have secured 11 of their 12 points against clubs in the perceived “Big Six” and Aston Villa, who are competing in the Champions League, and did not deserve the scoreline to be as close.

Alonso is the latest Chelsea manager to become embroiled in chaos before Christmas and four defeats from five league matches will not make happy reading for the hierarchy.

His defence appear to be nervous wrecks and in his desperation to toughen them up he opted to play Moisés Caicedo in what was a peculiar line-up.

Chelsea have conceded 23 goals in the league and until they improve that record, Alonso will find it impossible to retain the club’s backing.

“Everyone in the club needs to stick together and we have to deal with it,” he said. “We are going through a difficult moment with solidity and confidence, we need to find solutions.

“Everyone in the team is needed and I am thinking about the next games and we will see [if Fofana is picked for the next game]. We need to support everyone and if we don’t, things will get more complicated.”

Forest responded after their insipid performance at Bournemouth last weekend to secure another notable home result for Oliver Glasner.

He must be hoping that Forest’s owner, Evangelos Marinakis, turns up for every game.

Marinakis was in attendance for only the second time this season and, on his last visit, witnessed a stirring victory over Manchester City.

Morgan Gibbs-White scored twice to win the private battle of the England No 10s, with Chelsea’s Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers both ineffective.

Glasner said: “We feel we are heading in the right direction but there is still a lot to do. Twelve points from 12 games is still not satisfying for us, but wins like this help us show the players that it is working.

“If you have back-to-back wins against City and Chelsea you must be doing many things really well.”

Chelsea are never far away from a crisis and this feels like a big night for Xabi Alonso.

Three defeats in the last four Premier League games, including a thrashing by Leeds in their last match, has cranked up the pressure.

This was always likely to be a long-term project, however, and Chelsea remain convinced Alonso will lead them into a bright new era.

Until then, there are going to be some tricky times ahead. Chelsea are as wildly unpredictable as the team they face this evening at the City Ground.

They would leapfrog Coventry regardless of the margin of victory, as they already have a better goal difference.

A draw would see them remain 17th, while a really heavy defeat might see them fall to 18th.

Glasner conceded, in his own press conference, that he had hoped for better results so far this season.

He said: “We wanted and expected more to be honest, but it is still early. We look at what we need to improve and work on it. I’m no magician, I have no dust I can spread at the training ground.

“From my experience, everything is hard work and we need to improve our individual mistakes and defence. We need to improve our efficiency in attack and set pieces. We still haven’t scored from a set piece.”

He added that the club wanted a good atmosphere for the evening kick-off, saying that, “is what we want and need. Friday night under the flood lights - it’s crucial. Our fans want a great weekend.”

Earlier in the week, Chelsea defender Wesley Fofana said he could now “laugh” about a recent penalty miss against Liverpool in the Carabao Cup.

While the statement went down badly amongst some supporters, Fofana has apologised, and Alonso told a pre-match press conference he was ready to move on.

He told journalists: “Absolutely, we have addressed that with him and for sure it was unfortunate.

“He apologised, he knows it was not right the moment, it was not right the content, we are here to take things seriously and he said that it’s not going to be repeated and we know that it’s something that we don’t want, these kind of things, and they are not going to be repeated for sure.”

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea.

The City Ground hosts the Premier League clash tonight, with two sides who are both falling short of expectations.

Forest head coach Oliver Glasner brought with him a sense of optimism after he left Crystal Palace, but the club are just outside the bottom three, sitting in 17th position with only nine points. As things stand, they are only clear of 18th-placed Sunderland because of superior goal difference.

Beneath them, Glasner’s former club Palace are bottom, two points away from them, and then Manchester United come in 19th, a single point behind. With Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino now installed at Selhurst Park and Old Trafford, respectively, the pressure could soon be felt yet more keenly.

There have been flashes of encouragement, with a 3-1 win over Manchester City in early November, spearheaded by a brace from Liam Delap, who left Chelsea in the summer. However, last Saturday they lost 2-0 at Bournemouth to dent any nascent momentum, and the match was the sixth in 11 league games where the club have failed to score. Forest have scored nine times this season, with only Sunderland having a worse record in attack.

Chelsea’s Xabi Alonso has also endured a tough time of late. They were trounced 4-1 against Leeds United at home on Saturday, despite taking the lead in the first half.

That worrying collapse was the fourth loss in five league matches, and it followed a 1-0 defeat against Sunderland at the Stadium of Light before the recent international break.

There is speculation that Chelsea will move for a central defender in January, with 20 goals conceded in the Premier League so far.

Chelsea are currently in eighth place in the league with 16 points, five points behind Liverpool in fourth. Tonight, they could leapfrog Bournemouth, who are in fifth, two points ahead of them. Another loss, though, could see them in the bottom half once the weekend’s fixtures are completed.

Marseille head coach Bruno Genesio said “we are living through violent times” after five Levski Sofia fans were hospitalised following violent clashes before their Europa League encounter with the French side.

Groups of supporters threw projectiles and flares and French outlet L’Equipe reported that there were Nazi salutes observed in the away section.

Ten minutes before kick-off at the Stade Velodrome a group of Marseille fans broke through into the away stand, which housed around 500 fans.

In the ensuing clashes five people, all Bulgarian, were injured and taken to hospital “with eye injuries, head trauma and a dislocated shoulder”, according to the Marseille police prefecture, while six others were treated on-site for more superficial injuries.

The police force said there was “no information at this stage regarding any arrests”.

Security were able to restore order and the game kicked off on time, although there were further incidents later on, particularly at half-time.

Genesio said: “We are living through violent times in our society, so this is very, very regrettable.” Julio Velazquez, head coach of the Bulgarian domestic champions, said: “It's a very regrettable episode. These are incidents which are unacceptable for football.”

The Bulgarian Football Union condemned the violence and said it had referred the incident to UEFA, calling for the harshest possible sanctions. It also demanded full cooperation and transparency from French authorities in investigating the attacks and identifying those responsible.

Levski said the club's priority is the safety and well-being of its fans. A statement read: “What happened tonight is particularly alarming given the extraordinary security measures put in place by the French authorities, as well as the restrictions imposed on our travelling supporters—restrictions that the club had already formally contested with UEFA.

“Despite the risks identified by the club prior to the match, the measures taken failed to provide adequate protection for our fans. This is completely unacceptable.”

Marseille also condemned the violence and said it is conducting “a thorough analysis of the circumstances in which these incidents took place.”

Bulgarian President Iliana Yotova called for those responsible to be held accountable and Prime Minister Rumen Radev said he had spoken to French president Emmanuel Macron about the violence at a European summit in Brussels.

A spokesperson for Macron’s office said: “He condemned in the strongest possible terms these acts of violence targeting Bulgarian supporters, which have no place in sport or in public spaces, and assured the Prime Minister that these acts would not go unpunished.”

Marseille won the game 1-0, with Amine Gouiri scoring a 28th-minute penalty.

Sunday’s bruising 4-0 defeat at Anfield exposed the scale of the rebuild facing Mauricio Pochettino at Manchester United.

For all the scrutiny aimed at Man United’s midfield and attack, it is the fragility at the back that is of greatest concern - the club have now conceded more goals than any other side in Europe's top five leagues this season.

With the January transfer window fast approaching, Fulham’s Calvin Bassey - often linked with an Old Trafford move - is rapidly playing himself into contention for a switch.

Man United’s need for centre-half reinforcements could hardly be more urgent after the weekend's display. Matthijs de Ligt looked worryingly off the pace against Liverpool, struggling with his turning circle and repeatedly caught out whenever Andoni Iraola's side broke at speed.

The long-term picture looks increasingly bleak, too. Lisandro Martinez is widely expected to move on at the end of the season after previously speaking out publicly against the club, leaving a left-footed vacancy at the heart of defence.

Across the rest of Pochettino’s central defensive options, there is a lack of ready-made solutions. Leny Yoro, who endured a miserable afternoon of his own on Merseyside, and Ayden Heaven are both still very junior in their development, while Harry Maguire isn't getting any younger.

Throwing teenagers and early-20-somethings into an Old Trafford pressure cooker every week is no recipe for climbing the table, nor can Man United rely indefinitely on an ageing veteran to bail them out, as Maguire has done so consistently in the past.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

That is why Bassey ticks so many boxes for Man United’s new era under Pochettino.

Turning 27 on New Year’s Eve, the Nigeria international is entering his prime years as a defender. And having racked up more than 100 Premier League appearances since arriving in west London from Ajax in 2023, he brings the sort of battle-hardened top-flight pedigree Man United are crying out for.

In doing so, he removes the adaptation risk that has plagued so many overseas Old Trafford arrivals. His commanding display in Fulham’s 1-1 draw away at Manchester City on Saturday makes the appeal obvious; Bassey has good recovery pace, is dominant in physical duels, and comfortable defending wide channels.

Bassey won't cost the earth either as his initial four-year contract at Craven Cottage expires next summer, and although Fulham hold an option to extend his stay by a further 12 months, his contractual situation keeps any potential fee firmly within reach for a club of Man United's stature and commercial acumen.

Fulham are understandably eager to tie him down to fresh terms, but the lure of spearheading Pochettino’s Old Trafford reboot may prove hard to resist.

In FourFourTwo's view, if Bassey maintains his current level over the coming weeks, don't rule out a January approach.

A referee has hit back at claims he was “drunk” while officiating an AFC Champions League Two match.

Footage has been widely shared on social media of Syrian referee Hanna Hattab looking visibly disoriented during a match between Iran's Gol Gohar and Al Jazira of the United Arab Emirates.

One particular incident raised eyebrows when Hattab showed a yellow card to Al Jazira’s goalkeeper for a foul that happened close to the halfway line, 40 yards away from him.

Hattab was then replaced at half-time with the fourth official taking over for the remainder of the game, which Al Jazira won 1-0.

Reports claimed Gol Gohar staff accused the referee of being drunk following erratic decision-making as similar accusations flooded in online.

But Hattab, who is part of the AFC's elite refereeing group, has refuted the allegations as “insult and defamation”, threatening legal action.

“I also confirm my full right to take all legal and judicial measures against anyone who published or made a statement or contributed to the insult and defamation of me, regardless of their position or status, whether they are an individual, an institution, or a sports entity.”

He also said he would issue a further statement following contact with the Syrian Arab Football Federation (SFA) which will “clarify all the details and facts related to what happened ... with full transparency and clarity.”

Omani journalist Issa Said, who covers Asian football, has since claimed on social media that what happened to Hattab was "due to a drop in his blood sugar, which caused him to lose concentration and focus".

The SFA have also put out a statement standing in support of Hattab, while stating it has requested his medical report from the match.

“The Main Referees Committee of the Syrian Arab Football Federation confirms that it stands in full support of international referee Mr Hana Khattab regarding the incident he was subjected to, following reassurance about his health,” it said.

“This comes after the committee was reassured of his well-being, following a number of discussions on social media concerning the incident. The committee emphasises its full support for him and its commitment to following up on the matter in all its details and developments.

“In this regard, the committee has requested that the Syrian Football Referees Committee provide the medical report relating to the referee, the match observers' report and the referee assessor's report. This is in order to establish the circumstances of the incident accurately and comprehensively and to complete the necessary procedures in this matter.

“The committee also confirms that it will provide the relevant authorities and the public with the findings as soon as the requested reports are received, in order to ensure accuracy and to obtain information from official sources.”

But beyond this campaign, his future remains uncertain, with manager Mikel Arteta even recently alluding to the teenager's struggles at Signal Iduna Park.

Nwaneri became the Premier League's youngest-ever player in 2022 at the age of 15 – with Max Dowman later taking that record – before establishing himself in the 2024/25 season as a serious option on the right wing for the Gunners.

#911. Europa League match suspended after police clashes over Palestine banner

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute and restarted 30 minutes later

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

The Europa League game between Besiktas and Israel's Hapoel Beer-Sheva was suspended for around 30 minutes on Thursday when police clashed with fans of the Turkish club after they displayed a banner in support of Palestine.

The game, being played on neutral ground in Batumi, Georgia, was halted in the 26th minute but restarted after the interruption.

Turkey’s Haberturk broadcaster said Georgian police used pepper spray against the Besiktas fans, who also unfurled a Palestinian flag, prompting referee referee Morten Krogh to stop the game with the score 0-0.

In a statement, Besiktas accused the Georgian security forces of using “disproportionate” force against supporters before and during the game.

Georgian police entered the stands and ⁠used pepper spray on Besiktas fans, Turkish outlet NTV reported.

“We strongly condemn the security forces for their use of disproportionate force against our fans,” the club said. “We also extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our fans affected by these incidents.”

The report added that Turkish fans chanted “Down with Israel” and that Besiktas players and director of football Onder Ozen spoke to supporters before play restarted to calm the situation.

The Turkish Football Federation condemned the treatment of Besiktas supporters on X, saying they were subjected to unacceptable behaviour and discrimination. It said it would press for an investigation.

The TFF’s statement read: “We strongly condemn the unacceptable attitudes, conduct and interference directed at Beşiktaş supporters, both inside and outside the stadium, before and during our club’s Uefa Europa League match against Hapoel Beer-Sheva in Georgia.

“No practice that disregards the universal values of sport, human dignity, mutual respect and the principles of fair play, or that involves discrimination, exclusion or security failures, can be tolerated.

“Nor can there be any question of remaining silent in the face of such conduct, which endangers our supporters’ safety and targets their fundamental rights and freedoms.

“As the Turkish Football Federation, we declare unequivocally that we will follow this matter to its conclusion to ensure that the events are fully investigated, those responsible are identified and the necessary sanctions are imposed without delay.

“There must be no tolerance for covering up these events, allowing those responsible to evade accountability or permitting similar violations to recur.

“We emphasize that we stand firmly with our club, Besiktas, and our supporters, who faced a series of problems, particularly serious security failures, and extend our best wishes for a speedy recovery to all our supporters subjected to interference and mistreatment.

“Let no one forget that we will not remain silent in the face of disrespect, discrimination and security violations directed at representatives and supporters of Turkish football.

“We will act decisively on national and international platforms to ensure that all necessary steps are taken, particularly with Uefa, and that those responsible are held accountable.”

Turkish clubs echoed the sentiments of the TFF, with Besiktas’ rivals Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor all among those to stand with the club.

“We do not accept Turkish clubs being denied the right to play their home matches in their own country, in front of their own fans, when facing clubs from the occupying state of Israel,” Trabzonspor wrote in a statement.

“We do not consider Uefa’s double standards on this issue acceptable. We also strongly condemn the disproportionate intervention by security forces against Besiktas fans in Georgia this evening.”

The ⁠officiating team and the Besiktas players ‌left ​the pitch before ‌the game restarted.

Earlier, the Besiktas players refused to shake hands with their Hapoel counterparts, the state-run Anadolu Agency reported.

Hapoel Beer-Sheva and Israel FA had not commented on the incident at the time of publishing.

#910. Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

#909. From sketch to publication-ready flowchart: how AI tools can bridge the gap

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Ensar Aydemir is an endocrinologist at Sultan 1. Murat State Hospital in Edirne, Türkiye. X: @dreaydemir

Artificial-intelligence tools can speed up the process of generating publication-ready flowcharts. Credit: -MG-/Getty

When making a scientific diagram, whether I am outlining a clinical study, planning a flowchart or mapping a signalling pathway, I often start in the same way: with a pen and a piece of paper.

Sketching by hand is fast. I can draw a box, cross something out and reorganize a whole idea without thinking about fonts, alignment or software menus. At this stage, my aim is not to make the figure beautiful, it is to work out the logic.

Turning that rough sketch into a clean figure for a manuscript can be surprisingly tedious, however. Text boxes need to line up; arrows need to connect properly; and fonts, spacing and colours must be consistent. A diagram that took five minutes to draw might take an hour or longer to recreate digitally.

Multimodal artificial-intelligence tools can shorten this process. Rather than asking an AI model to create the final scientific image, I use it as a translator. The model reads my sketch, interprets its structure and converts it into editable diagram code that I can open in a vector-based editor, such as Draw.io — a free application for making diagrams.

This distinction matters. I do not want AI to invent a figure for me; I want it to help me to digitize a figure that I have already designed.

One tempting approach is to provide a description to an image-generation model and ask for a polished scientific figure.

For research diagrams, this can create more problems than it solves. Text might be misspelt, arrows misdirected and pathways altered. More importantly, the resulting image is usually flat (that is, the text, images and background are merged together), making it mostly uneditable. For diagrams in research publications, if a reviewer later asks you to alter it, you might have to start from scratch.

A better option is to ask a multimodal language model — for example, Google’s Gemini — to turn your idea into a structured diagram format, such as Draw.io-compatible XML or Mermaid syntax. The output can then be imported into a diagram editor, in which every box, label and connector remains editable.

In this workflow, AI is less an illustrator than a compiler: a programming tool that translates human-readable instructions into code that a computer can run. My sketch is the source, and Draw.io XML is the output.

Focus first on the structure of your figure. I roughly sketch the important nodes, branches and connections without worrying about visual polish. For a clinical study, these might include eligibility criteria, treatment groups and follow-up visits. For a laboratory workflow, they might represent experimental stages or decision points.

The key is to make the relationships clear. What box comes first? Where does the pathway split? Which arrow connects to which endpoint? If the logic is ambiguous to a human reader, it will be ambiguous to the AI model, too.

Once the sketch is complete, I photograph it, upload the image to a vision-enabled language model and provide a detailed prompt. For instance:

“Recreate the uploaded hand-drawn figure as a clean, editable academic flowchart in Draw.io-compatible XML format. Preserve the original structure as faithfully as possible, including box positions, arrows, dashed connectors, side boxes, branching pattern, and text content. This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task. Use a plain white background, thin dark slate-grey borders, white box fills, thin connector lines, clean sans-serif text, and no shadows, gradients, or decorative elements. Make it publication-quality while keeping it recognizably the same diagram.”

The instruction “This is a reconstruction task, not a redesign task” is crucial. Scientific diagrams are not the place for creative completion. I want the model to reconstruct my structure, not improve it on my behalf.

Note also that this prompt indicates what the model should not change. I explicitly ask it to preserve wording, branching relationships and directionality. If the diagram contains important numbers, doses or time points, I check each one manually.

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03513-1

Newcastle United star Sven Botman has been banned from driving after he was caught using his mobile phone at the wheel.

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) confirmed that Botman, 26, pleaded guilty at Newcastle Magistrates Court on Wednesday.

The Dutch international defender was given six penalty points and disqualified from driving for six months, as these were added to points he had already accrued.

The MoJ said Botman was fined £900 and ordered to pay £400 costs and a £360 surcharge.

Court documents show that Botman was in a Land Rover on the A189 Haddricks Mill Road, in Newcastle, on 17 September when he was spotted using his phone.

According to The Sun, the court heard he was filmed by a cyclist while he was stationary in traffic.

The Dutch centre-half was signed by Newcastle in a £32 million deal from French club Lille during the summer of 2022.

Since signing for the Magpies, Botman has made 124 appearances and was part of the squad that won the League Cup in 2025, their first major trophy in decades.

Are the Premier League’s London clubs at an advantage? Arsenal prepare to put that unique theory to the test

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Having made their longest Premier League away trip of the season to Newcastle last week, Arsenal can settle into familiar surroundings for the festive period: the Gunners don’t leave London again until mid-January when they travel to Hull.

Between now and then, Arsenal’s longest away day takes them just 22 kilometres to Brentford - Google Maps says the average person could walk from the Emirates to the Gtech in under four hours, never mind a professional footballer.

That’s the third of 11 straight games in the capital for the Gunners, which will become 12 if they’re drawn at home in the third round of the FA Cup, beginning with Tuesday’s Champions League clash against Borussia Dortmund. Recent history suggests an interesting theory about such home comforts.

Eleven games into their title defence, Arsenal sit second in the Premier League away table with four wins, one draw and one defeat from six games on the road. Not that it’s anything new for the Gunners to occupy such heights: they’ve boasted the top flight’s best away record in each of the last four seasons.

And that comes with the territory of being a London club. Across the last 10 Premier League campaigns not impacted by pandemic crowd restrictions (so excluding 2019/20 and 2020/21), only once have more clubs from London had a bottom-half away record than a top-half away record. That was last term, when four of the seven London clubs finished in the bottom 10 of the away table (Crystal Palace, Brentford, Fulham and West Ham).

In each of the other nine seasons in question, at least 57 per cent of the Premier League’s London clubs have finished with one of the best 10 away records in the division; in 2016/17, all five of them did (Chelsea, Tottenham, Arsenal, Palace and West Ham).

So, is it an advantage to be a London club?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

There’s not really a simple answer to that question (sorry), but we can still pull together some interesting takeaways.

This season, the average Premier League club will travel 153 kilometres for an away fixture. For two clubs, that average climbs to over 300km: the league’s two most north-easterly sides, Sunderland (350km) and Newcastle (347km), and the most south-westerly, Bournemouth (317km). Conversely, one side will travel a touch under 200km on average: Coventry (198km) – in that sense, you might consider the Sky Blues the ultimate Midlands club.

But the top-flight’s six London clubs all sit in the bottom eight of the league in terms of average away travel distance, with Palace travelling the furthest (227km) and Spurs the least far (202km). And the very fact that those sides account for just over a quarter of the division means short trips are a regular occurrence.

And for Arsenal, this 11-match stretch that sees them go no further than Brentford could not fall at a better time than the notoriously hectic festive period – certainly when it comes to maximising recovery time between fixtures, which come thick and fast an average of one game every 4.2 days between now and January 5 (though it’s worth noting that turnaround is still below the UEFA-recommended minimum window of five days between matches).

Could the timing of Arsenal’s London residency, so to speak, prove crucial to another successful Premier League title push? Well, they’re already six points clear at the top and look like they could walk it, given Manchester City’s dramatic recent drop-off, but minimising time spent on the road during one of the busiest stages of the campaign seems unlikely to work to their detriment.

That being said, a quick word on Chelsea: the Blues have left London three times all season but are languishing in mid-table in the Premier League and are out of the Carabao Cup. So, maybe there’s something to be said for getting out of town on a more regular basis. Besides, it’s not like elite-level players these days are travelling in anything less than luxury, is it?
